<system-reminder>
## Stored Secrets
- Before declaring that API tokens, passwords, or cloud credentials are unavailable, run `cortex secret list` to see stored secret keys.
- Use stored secrets with bash inline injection: `VAR="<storeKey>" cmd ...`. The client resolves <storeKey> at execution time and the secret value is not written into the transcript.
- On Windows (PowerShell), the prefix syntax is identical ΓÇö `MY_VAR="<storeKey>" cmd` ΓÇö but reference the variable inside the command as `$env:MY_VAR`, not `$MY_VAR` (e.g. `MY_TOKEN="<my-token>" curl.exe -u "user:$env:MY_TOKEN" https://...`).
- Do NOT embed `<storeKey>` directly in command arguments ΓÇö it must appear as the `VAR="<storeKey>"` prefix so the client can resolve it before the shell runs.
- Do NOT ask the user to paste secret values in chat. If a required key is missing, tell the user to add it via /secrets.
- Do NOT simulate credentialed external-service work when a relevant stored secret exists.
- For delegated credentialed work, use a full-capability `general-purpose` subagent and explicitly tell it to run `cortex secret list` and use inline injection. Do not assign non-GitHub credential consumers such as Databricks, GCP, curl, psql, or aws to Explore.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
Use `enter_plan_mode` proactively for non-trivial implementation tasks. If unsure, err on the side of planning.

WHEN TO PLAN ΓÇö enter plan mode when ANY of these apply:
- Multiple files to create or modify
- Task spans multiple layers, modules, or components
- Detailed requirements with business rules, formulas, or tiered logic
- Multiple reasonable approaches with real tradeoffs
- Architectural or behavioral impact on the system
- Exploration needed before implementing
- Design choices where user preferences matter

Once you understand the scope, call `enter_plan_mode` immediately ΓÇö do not continue exploring or implementing.

Do NOT enter plan mode for:
- Small, obvious fixes (typos, one-line bugs, minor tweaks)
- Single-file changes with clear, fully specified behavior
- Tasks where the user specified the exact code change
- Pure research or "what/where is X?" questions with no code changes
- Executing steps from an already-confirmed plan
- Personal preferences or memory/rule saves
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
IMPORTANT: For Snowflake operations, use the `cortex` CLI via bash instead of individual Snowflake tools. ## Cortex CLI
Use `cortex <command>` for Snowflake operations. All output is JSON. Use `--help` on any command. Do not use `snow sql` when an equivalent `cortex` command exists.

**Key commands:**
- `cortex connections list|set <name>` ΓÇö manage connections
- `cortex search object "<query>" [--types=...]` ΓÇö search Snowflake catalog objects (table, view, database, schema, function, semantic-view, agent, streamlit, external-table, external-database, external-schema, bi-object, business-ontology, stream, stage, task, pipe, skill, plugin) use --help for all supported types; `--types=skill` / `--types=plugin` search the skill/plugin catalog (same backends as `cortex skill find` / `cortex plugin find`)
- `cortex search table-details "DB.SCHEMA.TABLE"` ΓÇö look up detailed table metadata (all columns, data types, join patterns, usage stats)
- `cortex search marketplace "<query>" [--marketplace-type=TYPE]` ΓÇö search Snowflake Marketplace listings (TYPE: public (default), internal, or all)
- `cortex semantic-views discover|list|describe|search|ddl` ΓÇö semantic view discovery (IMPORTANT***: Search for semantic views BEFORE writing SQL to answer data centric questions)
- `cortex search docs "<query>"` ΓÇö search Snowflake docs. IMPORTANT: run this FIRST for ANY Snowflake question ΓÇö your built-in knowledge is often stale, so answer from results, not memory. If a result's content is truncated, use web_fetch on that result's Markdown URL to read the full page.
- `cortex reflect <file.yaml> [--target-schema DB.SCHEMA]` ΓÇö validate semantic models
- `cortex agents discover|list|describe|search` ΓÇö agent discovery (check BEFORE writing complex queries)
- `cortex lineage <DB.SCHEMA.NAME> [--direction upstream|downstream|both] [--distance 1..5] [--tree]` ΓÇö list upstream sources/downstream consumers; use before refactoring/deprecating and to find pre-aggregated rollups for analytical SQL
- `cortex analyst query "<question>" --model=<yaml>|--view=<view>` ΓÇö query via Cortex Analyst
- `cortex artifact create notebook|file <name> <path>` ΓÇö upload artifacts
- `cortex env detect [--dir=<path>]` ΓÇö detect Python environment
- `cortex secret store|list|delete` ΓÇö manage secrets

Do NOT use `cortex fdbt` ΓÇö use the native `fdbt` tool instead.
Do NOT use `cortex --bypass --print` - use your built-in mechanisms to execute SQL or run a subagent instead.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
## Snowflake Object Discovery

When the task requires finding or identifying a Snowflake object/asset and the user has NOT pinned an exact identifier, delegate to the `snowflake-object-discovery` subagent to locate it ΓÇö this is the default and expected way to find objects, ahead of hand-rolling `cortex search` or writing exploratory SQL yourself. It covers any supported object: tables, views, semantic views, Cortex Agents, Streamlit apps, functions, databases/schemas, BI objects, streams, stages, tasks, pipes, and Marketplace listings. 

For ANY analytical SQL ΓÇö aggregations, counts, DAU/MAU, time-series, dashboards, "find X by Y", "what tables trackΓÇª" ΓÇö delegate FIRST to find the right table/semantic view, then write SQL against what it returns.

Run discovery to ground yourself BEFORE answering with ad-hoc INFORMATION_SCHEMA/ACCOUNT_USAGE SQL, and before building anything new.

A display name is NOT a pinned identifier: values like `Northstar` or `Annual Report` still need discovery ΓÇö only an exact FQN or object name counts as pinned.

```
task(subagent_type: "snowflake-object-discovery", prompt: "Find the best object for: <user request verbatim>\n\nno_discovery_reminder: true")
```

- ALWAYS include the literal `no_discovery_reminder: true`. Pass only what the user explicitly said ΓÇö add no interpretation of your own.
- The reply leads with a structured Primary block (`primary_identifier`, `object_type`, and an `agentId`) plus optional alternates. Use the `primary_identifier` **exactly as written** ΓÇö never invent, swap, or re-canonicalize database/schema/name segments, and do not substitute an alternate. The subagent saw all the options and chose this one.
- If you believe the primary is wrong (columns do not support the metric, the object is the wrong type, or your SQL returns nothing), do NOT pick another identifier yourself ΓÇö resume the SAME session with `resume: "<agentId>"` and a refined prompt explaining what went wrong. Resuming keeps prior inspection state and is cheaper.
- When you present the answer, name the object FQN(s) you relied on ΓÇö even for analytical or single-number answers ΓÇö so it is clear which asset produced the result.
</system-reminder>

You have `tgrep` for semantic/keyword code search ΓÇö prefer it over grep/glob for finding relevant files by meaning. tgrep loads on demand: if it isn't already in your available tools, use tool_search to load it FIRST, then call `tgrep` with a `query`. Do not call tgrep before it is loaded.
</system-reminder>

Tools: cron_create (5-field cron + prompt), cron_delete (by ID), cron_list. Session-scoped, local timezone, max 50, 3-day expiry. Users can also use /loop.

Use PowerShell cmdlets or their common aliases (ls, cat, cd, echo work as aliases).

Generate commands compatible with this shell. Do NOT generate bash-specific syntax.

# Risk & Compliance Copilot ΓÇö Solution Plan

**Problem statement:** Banking/NBFC teams manage real-time fraud, liquidity and credit risk, and
regulatory reporting (AML, Basel, local regulations) largely manually today. Build a copilot that
surfaces risk and fraud signals and produces audit-ready regulatory outputs from natural language
questions.

**Judging focus:** Real World Relevance ┬╖ Technical Execution ┬╖ Solution Completeness
**Platform requirement:** CoCo (CLI/Desktop) used across planning, development, execution, and testing.

| | |
|---|---|
| Status | Draft ΓÇö under revision |
| Last updated | 2026-09-19 |
| Owner | ΓÇö |

> **Verification flag.** Domain structure and typologies below are written from general knowledge.
> **Exact thresholds, form numbers, filing deadlines, and feed URLs change and must be verified**
> against current RBI / FIU-IND / BCBS / OFAC sources before being hardcoded. See ┬º8.

---

## Contents

1. [What the prompt is actually asking for](#1-what-the-prompt-is-actually-asking-for)
2. [Domain research: the four pillars](#2-domain-research-the-four-pillars)
3. [Architectural principles](#3-architectural-principles)
4. [Data model and ontology](#4-data-model-and-ontology)
5. [Data synthesis approach](#5-data-synthesis-approach)
6. [External inputs and refresh cadence](#6-external-inputs-and-refresh-cadence)
7. [Standout features, ranked](#7-standout-features-ranked)
8. [Scope and the demo spine](#8-scope-and-the-demo-spine)
9. [Research sources](#9-research-sources)
10. [Failure modes to design against](#10-failure-modes-to-design-against)
11. [Build sequence](#11-build-sequence)
12. [Open questions](#12-open-questions)

---

## 1. What the prompt is actually asking for

Read the requirement bullets closely and note what they do *not* ask for:

> "governed, explainable, evidence backed answers"
> "from signal to evidence to a documented finding or report"
> "audit ready regulatory outputs"

This is not natural-language BI. It asks for a system whose **unit of output is a defensible
artifact** ΓÇö something a compliance officer could hand to a regulator and survive questioning on.

That has a hard technical consequence. In BI, the answer *is* the deliverable. In compliance, the
answer is worthless without the chain behind it: which rule fired, on which rows, under which policy
clause, computed at which point in time, reviewed by whom.

**The chain is the product. The chat is the interface.**

Core mental model:

```
signal  ΓåÆ  case  ΓåÆ  evidence bundle  ΓåÆ  finding  ΓåÆ  artifact  ΓåÆ  attestation
(detect)  (group)   (gather + freeze)  (reason+cite) (draft)    (human sign-off)
```

Every stage is a **persisted object with an ID**, not a step in a prompt chain. If a stage exists
only inside an LLM context window, it is not auditable.

---

## 2. Domain research: the four pillars

Enough domain literacy that the vocabulary is right. For each pillar, the artifact matters most ΓÇö
the artifact is what we generate.

### 2.1 Fraud ΓÇö real-time, transaction-level

Typologies, roughly ordered by demo value:

- **Mule networks** ΓÇö accounts opened to receive and rapidly forward illicit funds. Signals:
  fan-in/fan-out ratio, pass-through velocity (in and out within minutes, near-zero retained
  balance), shared device/IP/phone/address across nominally unrelated accounts. **This is a graph
  problem** ΓÇö relevant to our depth story.
- **Account takeover (ATO)** ΓÇö credential compromise. Signal is behavioural discontinuity: new
  device + new geography + beneficiary added + limit raised + drain, in a short window.
- **Structuring / smurfing** ΓÇö breaking amounts into sub-threshold chunks. Many transactions
  clustered just below a known reporting threshold.
- **First-party / synthetic identity fraud** ΓÇö the borrower is the fraudster. Bust-out pattern:
  build good behaviour, max out, vanish.
- **Origination / loan fraud** ΓÇö falsified income docs, ghost borrowers, round-tripping between
  related parties.

*Artifact:* internal fraud case file + regulatory fraud reporting (India: Fraud Monitoring Returns
to RBI ΓÇö verify current form and timeline).

### 2.2 AML ΓÇö entity-level, periodic + event-driven

Risk-based regime: **KYC/CDD** at onboarding, **EDD** for high-risk (PEPs, high-risk jurisdictions,
complex ownership), **ongoing monitoring**, **sanctions/PEP screening**, **reporting**.

Under Indian law (PMLA), reporting goes to **FIU-IND**. Distinct report types: **CTR** (cash above
threshold), **STR** (suspicious transaction report), **CCR** (counterfeit currency), **NTR**
(non-profit transactions), **CBWTR** (cross-border wire transfers).

**The STR is the money shot.** It is narrative, evidence-backed, genuinely hand-written today, and
exactly "audit-ready regulatory output from natural language questions."

STR narrative structure to learn: who; which accounts; what pattern over what period; quantified;
why it is suspicious; what the institution did; what supports it.

Also model the distinction between an **alert**, a **case**, and a **filing decision** ΓÇö and that
most alerts correctly close with no action. A system that files on everything is broken. The
**"no STR warranted, and here is why"** path is as important as the filing path.

### 2.3 Liquidity risk ΓÇö as-of-date, balance-sheet level

- **LCR** ΓÇö high-quality liquid assets ├╖ net cash outflows under a 30-day stress scenario.
- **ALM / structural liquidity** ΓÇö assets and liabilities bucketed by maturity, cumulative gap
  limits per bucket. The classic NBFC failure mode: borrow short, lend long, get caught.
- **Behavioural vs contractual maturity** ΓÇö deposits do not all leave on contract date. These
  assumptions are a governance object in their own right.

*Artifact:* structural liquidity statement with bucketed gaps; LCR computation with component
breakdown; breach explanation.

### 2.4 Credit risk ΓÇö portfolio-level, daily staging

- **DPD buckets and SMA staging** ΓÇö SMA-0/1/2 as early warning before NPA.
- **NPA classification** ΓÇö substandard ΓåÆ doubtful ΓåÆ loss, with prescribed ageing.
- **ECL under Ind AS 109** ΓÇö Stage 1/2/3; 12-month vs lifetime expected loss; staging driven by
  "significant increase in credit risk."
- **Basel** ΓÇö Pillar 1 minimum capital (credit + market + operational RWA), Pillar 2 supervisory
  review / ICAAP, Pillar 3 disclosure. For Indian NBFCs the headline analogue is **CRAR**, with a
  Tier 1 sub-minimum, under RBI's Scale-Based Regulation layers.

*Artifact:* provisioning/staging report; CRAR computation; large-exposure and early-warning reporting.

### 2.5 The unifying insight

These four are normally built as four silos, and that **is** the institutional pain:

> The same entity is a fraud signal to one team, an AML subject to another, a credit deterioration
> to a third, and an exposure line to a fourth ΓÇö and nobody joins them.

That is our demo spine (┬º8).

---

## 3. Architectural principles

Five non-negotiable decisions.

### 3.1 Deterministic numbers, generated narrative

**The LLM must never compute a regulatory figure.** Not LCR, not CRAR, not a transaction total, not
an alert count. Every number comes from SQL over governed tables ΓÇö semantic views with verified
queries, so the same question always produces the same SQL.

The LLM's job: select, sequence, explain, cite, write prose. It consumes numbers as inputs it is
forbidden to alter.

Then add the step almost nobody adds: a **programmatic reconciliation check** that parses numerals
out of the generated narrative and asserts each appears in the underlying result set. If a number in
the prose is not traceable to a query result, the artifact is rejected and regenerated.

Ten lines of code; the single most credible thing to show a judge with a risk background.

### 3.2 Point-in-time discipline

Every finding is stamped with `as_of_timestamp` and the query that produced it. Snowflake closes the
loop in a way most platforms cannot: **Time Travel lets us re-execute the exact query
`AT(TIMESTAMP => <as_of>)` and demonstrate the finding reproduces.**

That is a genuine audit-ready capability, not a claim. **Demo it explicitly** ΓÇö regenerate an old
finding live and show byte-identical numbers.

Also: make the findings table append-only (supersede via revisions, never update) so the audit trail
cannot be quietly rewritten.

### 3.3 Policy text as a control, not as context

- **Weak version:** RAG over policy PDFs, paste a paragraph in as "context."
- **Strong version:** extract policy into **structured, effective-dated rules** ΓÇö
  `{clause_id, source_doc, page, effective_from, applicability, metric, operator, threshold, action}`.

Then:
- detection rule and narrative citation reference the **same** clause ID
- a threshold change is a data change, not a code change
- we can answer "which controls implement clause X?" and "which findings depend on a clause that
  just changed?"

This is policy-as-code *derived from* policy-as-text, and it enables the best standout feature (┬º7.2).

Tools: `AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT` for layout-aware extraction, `AI_EXTRACT` for structured fields.
Relevant skills: `document-intelligence`, `ai-functions-pipeline-builder`.

### 3.4 Two-speed architecture, stated explicitly

Fraud is seconds. Basel is as-of-date. Do not pretend they share a pipeline.

- **Fast lane** ΓÇö Snowpipe Streaming ΓåÆ streams ΓåÆ low-target-lag dynamic tables for transaction
  scoring and velocity features.
- **Slow lane** ΓÇö batch dynamic tables at daily/monthly lag for balance-sheet aggregation, staging,
  returns.
- **Shared** ΓÇö the same conformed party/account dimension. Both lanes resolve to one `party_id`.

Saying "these have different SLAs and here is why" is a maturity signal. Bonus: make a fast-lane
fraud signal materialise into the slow lane's exposure view ΓÇö the join nobody does.

### 3.5 Maker-checker is a schema requirement

Regulatory filings legally require human sign-off with segregation of duties. Model it:

```
finding:     draft ΓåÆ under_review ΓåÆ approved ΓåÆ filed   (+ rejected, withdrawn)
attestation: finding_id, attestor, role, timestamp, comment, signature_hash
```

The agent proposes. A human attests. **The agent cannot transition to `filed`.**

Ten minutes of work; communicates more banking credibility than any feature.

---

## 4. Data model and ontology

Design before generating a row. Draft it in CoCo and keep the artifact ΓÇö it is planning-phase evidence.

| Entity | Why it exists |
|---|---|
| `Party` | Customer, counterparty, beneficial owner. Risk rating, PEP flag, KYC status, jurisdiction. Entity-resolution anchor. |
| `PartyRelationship` | PartyΓåöParty: ownership, shared device/IP/address/phone, fund flow. **Enables ring detection.** |
| `Account` | Owned by party; product type, balance, status. |
| `Transaction` | The spine. Debit/credit, channel, counterparty account, timestamp, amount, geo, device. |
| `Exposure` | Credit position: outstanding, limit, DPD, stage, collateral. |
| `Signal` | One rule/model firing on one entity at one time. Cheap, high-volume. |
| `Case` | Groups signals into an investigable unit. Owner, status, SLA clock. |
| `Evidence` | **Pointers, not copies:** `(case_id, ref_type, ref_id, query_id, as_of)`. |
| `Finding` | Reasoned conclusion. Cites evidence + policy clause. Versioned. |
| `PolicyClause` | Extracted rule from policy/circular text. Effective-dated. |
| `Artifact` | Generated output: STR draft, LCR statement, board memo. Links to finding. |
| `Attestation` | Human sign-off. Append-only. |

### 4.1 The critical modelling choice

**`Evidence` stores references, not values.** A copied number is a snapshot you must trust. A
`(txn_id, as_of_ts, query_id)` triple is **re-verifiable** ΓÇö which is the literal definition of
audit-ready.

### 4.2 Entity resolution

The whole value proposition collapses if the fraud team's customer and the credit team's borrower are
different rows. Build a deliberate `party_id` resolution step, document the match strategy, and make
uncertainty visible (**match confidence as a column**). Judges will ask.

### 4.3 Graph traversal

Mule-ring and related-party detection is graph traversal. Snowflake handles this with **bounded
recursive CTEs** over `PartyRelationship`. A depth-3 fund-flow ring with a shared-device edge is a
legitimately sophisticated query and a strong visual. Bound the depth; guard against cycles.

### 4.4 Semantic layer

Author **one semantic view per domain** (transactions/AML, exposures/credit, balance-sheet/liquidity)
ΓÇö not one god-view. Then invest heavily in **verified queries** for every regulatory metric: CRAR,
LCR, SMA counts, threshold-breach counts.

Verified queries are how "deterministic numbers" becomes real: the metric definition lives in the
semantic layer, version-controlled, not in a prompt. Skill: `agent-studio`.

---

## 5. Data synthesis approach

### 5.1 Decision: calibrated agent-based simulation with planted typologies

**Rejected: SMOTE.** Not a data generator. It interpolates minority-class *feature vectors* to
rebalance a training set. No concept of a graph (cannot create a mule ring), no concept of
double-entry (cannot keep a balance sheet tied), and interpolation can produce physically impossible
records. If used at all, it belongs inside a classifier's training step, never in dataset construction.

**Rejected: tabular GANs (CTGAN, TVAE).** Fatal premise problem ΓÇö they learn a distribution from
*real* data, and we have none by design. Training a GAN on data we fabricated is a laundering step
that adds zero information and **destroys the one asset we need: known ground truth.** Also: no
cross-table referential integrity, no graph topology, **mode-collapse precisely on rare events (and
fraud *is* the rare event)**, and unexplainable ΓÇö disqualifying when a judge asks "why is this
account suspicious?"

**Chosen: agent-based simulation.** What the field actually does ΓÇö the published simulators in this
domain (PaySim, AMLSim) are agent-based, not generative.

### 5.2 Comparison table (for the deck)

| Criterion | SMOTE | Tabular GAN | **Agent-based simulation** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Needs real training data | yes | **yes** | **no** |
| Ground-truth labels | partial | **none** | **exact, by construction** |
| Referential integrity across tables | no | no | **enforced** |
| Balance sheet / double-entry ties | no | no | **enforced** |
| Graph topology (mule rings) | no | no | **designed explicitly** |
| Rare-event fidelity | distorts | mode-collapses | **specified directly** |
| Explainable to an auditor | no | no | **yes ΓÇö documented rationale** |
| Reproducible | partial | hard to pin | **fixed seed ΓåÆ identical data** |
| Build time | low | high (train + tune) | **low** |

Rows 3ΓÇô6 are where the generative approaches fail and where this problem lives. Row 2 is the killer:
**without labels there is no precision/recall, no confusion matrix, no "Testing and validation" score.**

### 5.3 The honest concession, and its mitigation

Agent-based simulation is only as statistically rich as its assumptions. Do not hide this ΓÇö
**calibrate parameters from published aggregate statistics** rather than inventing them: amount
distributions, channel mix, time-of-day curves, DPD roll rates, sector NPA ratios, payment-rail
volume mixes. RBI payment-system data, NPCI volume stats, and published industry NPA/provisioning
ratios are public aggregates.

This upgrades the claim from "synthetic data" to **"calibrated simulation."**

### 5.4 Where generative AI does belong

The **unstructured layer** ΓÇö policy documents, circular text, KYC narratives, complaint text, prior
STR narratives. There, language variety *is* the value and there are no numbers to corrupt. Use
`AI_COMPLETE`, conditioned on the structured facts already planted, so text and data agree.

**Line for the deck:** *generative models where language variety adds value; deterministic simulation
where numbers and relationships must be provable.*

### 5.5 The hybrid architecture

| Layer | Method |
|---|---|
| Structured spine | deterministic seeded simulator |
| Typologies | planted, with held-out `ground_truth` table |
| Parameters | calibrated from public aggregate statistics |
| Unstructured layer | `AI_COMPLETE`, conditioned on planted structured facts |
| Validation | reconciliation tests (hard gate) + statistical plausibility checks |

### 5.6 Ground truth and measurement

For each typology, plant a known count and record it:

```
ground_truth: entity_id, typology, planted_at, severity, expected_detection
```

This enables precision, recall, and a confusion matrix over the detection logic ΓÇö **the entire
"Testing and validation" score**, and it converts "we built a thing" into "we built a thing and here
is how well it works."

### 5.7 Three things teams get wrong

1. **Base rates.** Real fraud is a fraction of a percent. At 30% everything looks easy and nothing is
   credible. Keep it honest so the metrics mean something.
2. **Referential consistency.** Balances must reconcile to transactions; exposures must roll up to
   portfolio totals; maturity buckets must sum to the balance sheet. If LCR does not tie to our own
   balance sheet, a judge who checks will find it. **Reconciliation suite runs as a gate.**
3. **Hard negatives.** Plant lookalikes that should *not* fire: a legitimate business with high cash
   velocity, a customer who legitimately travels, a seasonal borrower who legitimately goes 45 DPD
   and cures. Without these, precision is fake.

Also plant a **temporal narrative**, not just static anomalies: an account that looks normal,
degrades over weeks, then bursts. Point-in-time correctness only demonstrates itself against data
that changes over time.

### 5.8 Privacy note

Differential privacy and k-anonymity are for when you *hold* real data and must release it safely.
Our answer is stronger: **production data was never ingested, so the risk is eliminated rather than
mitigated.**

---

## 6. External inputs and refresh cadence

### 6.1 Decision: regulation is not a real-time feed

**Do not build, or claim, real-time regulatory ingestion.** It signals to a domain judge that we do
not understand the tempo of the work.

Regulatory change has a different clock: circulars publish irregularly, carry an **effective date
usually in the future**, and require **human legal interpretation** before becoming a control change.
Auto-activating a parsed threshold would be a compliance incident, not a feature.

### 6.2 Multi-clock design

| Layer | Clock | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Transactions / fraud signals | secondsΓÇôminutes | Snowpipe Streaming ΓåÆ streams ΓåÆ low-lag dynamic tables |
| **Sanctions / PEP / watchlists** | **daily, or on publication** | scheduled task ΓÇö these genuinely change often |
| Regulatory text (circulars, master directions) | **daily poll, human-gated promotion** | task ΓåÆ parse ΓåÆ diff ΓåÆ impact ΓåÆ review queue ΓåÆ approve ΓåÆ effective-dated activation |
| Prudential metrics (LCR, CRAR) | as-of-date | batch dynamic tables |
| Returns / filings | statutory calendar | scheduled task aligned to due dates |

**Critical rule:** the policy pipeline outputs a **proposed** rule change, never an activated one.
Ingest ΓåÆ extract ΓåÆ diff ΓåÆ impact analysis ΓåÆ compliance review queue ΓåÆ human approval ΓåÆ activation on
the clause's effective date. Same maker-checker principle as ┬º3.5, applied to the policy layer ΓÇö and
the review queue *is* the demo for ┬º7.2.

### 6.3 Real public sources worth wiring

> Listed from knowledge. **Verify current URLs, formats, and terms of use before building.**

**Best real external input: sanctions lists.** Genuinely public, machine-readable, updated on change,
and genuinely used in AML screening:

- **UN Security Council Consolidated List** ΓÇö XML, updated on change
- **OFAC SDN + consolidated lists** (US Treasury) ΓÇö XML/CSV, well documented, frequent
- **EU consolidated sanctions list**; **UK OFSI consolidated list**
- **MHA UAPA** designated individuals/organisations (India)

Ingesting the real UN or OFAC list is a strong credibility move ΓÇö actual regulatory data inside an
otherwise synthetic demo, free and legal to use.

**Scheduled, low-frequency, high-value:**
- **FATF high-risk and monitored jurisdictions** ΓÇö updated ~3├ù/year at plenaries. Perfect scheduled
  job; drives real risk-scoring logic.
- **RBI** circulars/notifications and Master Directions ΓÇö feeds exist; verify endpoints. Source for
  the circular watcher.
- **FIU-IND** reporting formats and guidance.
- **RBI reference rates** ΓÇö daily, if revaluation is in scope.

**Adjacent borrower-risk signals (optional depth):**
- MCA / IBBI insolvency filings against borrowers
- CERSAI security-interest registry
- Adverse-media screening ΓÇö a real AML requirement; public news APIs work
- Credit bureau data is **commercial, not public** ΓÇö note rather than pretend

**Check before scraping:** the Snowflake Marketplace carries sanctions, PEP, firmographic, and
adverse-media listings. Pulling a share beats scraping and is a legitimate ingenuity point.

### 6.4 Note on automation placement

`cortex automation` runs in a Snowflake-managed sandbox **with no local filesystem access**. That
suits this use case exactly: a circular watcher or sanctions refresh should write to Snowflake stages
and tables, not to a local repo.

---

## 7. Standout features, ranked

Mapped to the brief's bonus list, ordered by differentiation per unit effort.

### 7.1 Adversarial reviewer agent ΓÇö highest payoff

A final agent whose only job is to attack the artifact before a human sees it:

- Does every numeral in the narrative trace to a query result?
- Does every assertion cite evidence?
- Is every cited policy clause in effect on the as-of date?
- Is the evidence sufficient, or should this be "insufficient evidence"?
- Were contradictory signals ignored?

On failure the artifact is regenerated or downgraded to "needs analyst review."

Scores simultaneously on **multi-agent orchestration**, **guardrails and graceful fallback**, and
**testing/validation**. Best ROI on the entire list.

### 7.2 Regulatory change management ΓÇö most differentiated

Drop a new circular into a stage. The pipeline parses it, extracts changed clauses, diffs against
`PolicyClause`, then reports: **which controls are affected, which open findings relied on the
superseded clause, and what the numbers look like re-run under the new rule.**

A genuine, expensive, universal banking pain point; the natural payoff of ┬º3.3 and ┬º6.2. Run as a
scheduled automation to also cover unattended operation. Unlikely any other team does this.

### 7.3 One entity, four lenses

The demo structure ΓÇö see ┬º8.2. Scores directly on Solution Completeness.

### 7.4 MCP connectors chosen for workflow fit

Wire the ones that complete the loop, not the ones that are easy:

- **Jira** ΓÇö the case *is* a ticket. Opening an investigation creates it with the evidence bundle
  attached. This is how case management actually works.
- **Slack** ΓÇö alert the compliance channel; run maker-checker approval in-thread. Strong visual.
- **Google Drive / SharePoint** ΓÇö where circulars and filed reports actually live. Ingest from there;
  write the final PDF back.

Three connectors each serving a distinct workflow stage beats six that only read data.

### 7.5 Custom tools that take action

Register functions, not just retrieval: `open_case()`, `attach_evidence()`, `request_attestation()`,
`recompute_metric(as_of)`, `flag_account_for_review()`.

Stub the genuinely destructive ones (account freeze) behind an obvious mock **and say so** ΓÇö that is
a governance point in our favour, not a gap.

### 7.6 Guardrails, concretely

Beyond the reviewer:
- PII masking policies with role-based unmasking ΓÇö demo an analyst seeing masked data and a
  supervisor unmasking, with access logged
- **"insufficient evidence" as a first-class terminal outcome**, not an error
- confidence thresholds routing to human review rather than guessing
- read-only session scoping so the agent provably cannot mutate source data

### 7.7 Reusable skills

Three or four genuinely reusable, clearly documented skills. Note all are **generic** ΓÇö none is "our
demo, wrapped." That is the bar.

- `policy-to-rule-extractor` ΓÇö circular/policy PDF ΓåÆ structured effective-dated rules
- `evidence-bundle-builder` ΓÇö case ID ΓåÆ re-verifiable evidence pack with point-in-time query refs
- `regulatory-narrative-drafter` ΓÇö finding + evidence ΓåÆ cited narrative, with the numeric
  reconciliation gate built in
- `planted-typology-generator` ΓÇö synthetic data with ground-truth labels

### 7.8 Surfaces

CLI for the engineering/orchestration story, Streamlit for the compliance user, Slack for
alert-to-approval, Snowsight for the cloud-agent angle. **Same semantic layer and same findings
tables behind all of them** ΓÇö that is the point to land: one governed core, many surfaces.

---

## 8. Scope and the demo spine

### 8.1 Scope decision

Four domains built shallowly reads as thin.

- **Deep: Fraud + AML.** They share the transaction spine and the network/graph angle, so the
  marginal cost of the second is low, and AML yields the best artifact (STR).
- **One prudential metric, done properly: LCR *or* CRAR** ΓÇö not all of Basel. One is enough to prove
  the balance-sheet regulatory-output axis. Pick whichever the synthetic balance sheet supports most
  cleanly.
- **Credit risk as the bridge.** SMA/DPD staging is cheap and is the connective tissue ΓÇö it feeds
  both provisioning and the capital metric.

### 8.2 The demo spine ΓÇö one entity, four lenses

> A single synthetic counterparty. Fraud signals fire on pass-through velocity and a shared-device
> link to three other accounts. The investigation escalates to an AML case; the ring is traced with a
> graph query; the agent drafts a cited STR and the reviewer agent validates every number before a
> human attests. The same counterparty is a borrower ΓÇö the fraud finding triggers early-warning
> review, credit staging moves, provisioning changes, and the exposure flows through to the CRAR
> computation, which now sits closer to its floor. The agent explains the chain in one narrative,
> citing the transactions, the policy clauses, and the as-of timestamps.

**One entity, one story, four pillars, one evidence chain.** Far stronger than four disconnected
features, and it *is* the argument for why joining these silos matters ΓÇö the Real World Relevance score.

---

## 9. Research sources

### 9.1 Regulatory primary sources
> Verify current versions ΓÇö these get revised.

- RBI **Master Directions for NBFCs** under Scale-Based Regulation ΓÇö layer definitions, CRAR and
  Tier 1 minimums, applicability thresholds
- RBI **Master Direction on Fraud Risk Management** (consolidated, revised 2024) ΓÇö classification,
  reporting timelines, governance
- RBI **IRAC norms** ΓÇö DPD, SMA-0/1/2, NPA ageing
- RBI **ALM guidelines** ΓÇö maturity buckets, cumulative gap tolerances
- **PMLA + PML Rules**, and **FIU-IND** reporting formats ΓÇö CTR/STR/CCR/NTR/CBWTR structure
- **BCBS Basel III** framework and **Pillar 3 disclosure templates** ΓÇö structure and vocabulary
- **Ind AS 109** ΓÇö ECL staging criteria

### 9.2 Typology and control material

- **FATF** 40 Recommendations + typology reports ΓÇö canonical money-laundering vocabulary
- **Wolfsberg Group** statements and questionnaires ΓÇö precise control language to lift into the
  policy model
- **ACAMS** typology material ΓÇö practitioner-level red-flag catalogues

### 9.3 Snowflake capability research
Via `cortex search docs` and the relevant skills.

- dynamic tables (incremental refresh, target lag), streams, tasks, Snowpipe Streaming
- Cortex Analyst semantic views + verified queries
- `AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT`, `AI_EXTRACT`, `AI_CLASSIFY`, `AI_COMPLETE`
- Time Travel for point-in-time reproduction
- masking policies, row access policies, tags/classification
- recursive CTE patterns and their limits

---

## 10. Failure modes to design against

- **Chat-over-tables masquerading as a copilot** ΓÇö no evidence chain, no artifact, no sign-off.
- **The LLM computing regulatory figures** ΓÇö fatal with any judge who knows the domain.
- **No as-of discipline** ΓÇö numbers shift between demo runs and cannot be explained.
- **Policy RAG returning paragraphs** instead of clause-level, effective-dated rules.
- **Skipping maker-checker** ΓÇö an agent that files autonomously is, to a compliance audience, a
  compliance *incident*.
- **No measured accuracy** ΓÇö "it works" without a confusion matrix is unverifiable.
- **Vanity multi-agent** ΓÇö five agents passing text scores worse than three with distinct
  responsibilities and clean handoffs.
- **Perfect-path-only demo** ΓÇö show the refusal, show "insufficient evidence," show a false positive
  correctly closed with documented rationale. Graceful failure is on the scoring list explicitly and
  is the easiest place to stand out, because nobody rehearses it.
- **Claiming real-time regulatory ingestion** ΓÇö see ┬º6.1.
- **Using a GAN to generate the structured data** ΓÇö destroys ground truth; see ┬º5.1.

---

## 11. Build sequence

Generate CoCo evidence as a by-product rather than reconstructing it later: keep planning transcripts,
the ontology draft, semantic-view validation output, reconciliation test runs, the precision/recall
report, and automation definitions.

| # | Step | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Ontology + evidence-chain schema** | First. `Evidence`-as-pointers is load-bearing for everything downstream. |
| 2 | **Choose and document the synthesis approach** | Explicit and written down ΓÇö it is a slide. Record the reasoning against GAN/SMOTE. |
| 3 | **Build the simulator and the data** | See breakdown below. |
| 3a | ΓÇö calibrate parameters from public aggregate statistics | ┬º5.3 |
| 3b | ΓÇö deterministic seeded simulator for the structured spine | fixed RNG seed |
| 3c | ΓÇö plant typologies, hard negatives, temporal narrative; write `ground_truth` | ┬º5.6, ┬º5.7 |
| 3d | ΓÇö `AI_COMPLETE` the unstructured layer, conditioned on planted facts | ┬º5.4 |
| 3e | ΓÇö reconciliation + plausibility tests as a **hard gate** | ┬º5.7 |
| 4 | **Semantic views + verified queries** for every regulatory metric | Validate against NL questions now, not at the end. |
| 5 | **Detection layer** ΓÇö rules + graph queries | Scored against `ground_truth` from day one. |
| 6 | **Document lane** ΓÇö policy/circular parsing into effective-dated `PolicyClause` | ┬º3.3 |
| 7 | **External inputs and refresh cadence** | Sanctions/PEP, FATF list, circular watcher. Each on its own clock, **human-gated promotion**. ┬º6 |
| 8 | **Agent chain** ΓÇö signal ΓåÆ investigate ΓåÆ policy-map ΓåÆ draft ΓåÆ **review** | Build the reviewer early; it changes what the drafter must produce. |
| 9 | **Artifact generation + numeric reconciliation gate + attestation workflow** | ┬º3.1, ┬º3.5 |
| 10 | **Surfaces and MCP** | Last. Shallowest layer, most tempting to start with. |

**Discipline to hold:** do not build the Streamlit app first. It is the most visible layer and the
least load-bearing; time spent there early is time not spent on the evidence chain that differentiates us.

**Steps 2, 3a, and 7 were additions to the original plan.** Step 7 was the real gap ΓÇö without it the
policy layer is a static one-time load, which quietly kills the regulatory-change-management feature
(┬º7.2), our strongest differentiator.

---

This is a good question to ground before building. Let me walk through the current-state reality based on what the solution plan targets.

---

## Who does this work today

There are four distinct teams in a bank/NBFC, each operating largely in isolation:

**1. Fraud Operations (Transaction Monitoring)**
- **People:** Fraud analysts (L1 triage), fraud investigators (L2/L3), fraud operations manager
- **What they do:** Review automated alerts from a transaction monitoring system (TMS), decide real vs false positive, open a case, gather evidence, write an internal fraud case file, report to RBI per the Fraud Monitoring Return timeline
- **Pain:** Alert volumes are enormous, false positive rates run 95%+. L1 analysts spend most of their day clicking "close - not suspicious" with a note. The 5% that matter get buried.

**2. AML/CFT Compliance (Financial Crime)**
- **People:** AML analysts, MLRO (Money Laundering Reporting Officer), compliance officers
- **What they do:** Run KYC/CDD at onboarding, screen against sanctions and PEP lists, review transaction monitoring alerts that cross AML thresholds, investigate, and ΓÇö critically ΓÇö **write STRs by hand**. An STR is a structured narrative filed with FIU-IND explaining who did what, why it is suspicious, what evidence supports it, and what the institution did about it.
- **Pain:** STR drafting takes hours per case. The analyst pulls data from 4-6 systems (core banking, TMS, KYC platform, sanctions screening tool, case management, sometimes Excel), manually cross-references, and writes prose. The MLRO then reviews, sends back for revision, and eventually signs off. Turnaround is days to weeks.

**3. Credit Risk / Portfolio Management**
- **People:** Credit analysts, portfolio managers, provisioning team, Chief Risk Officer's office
- **What they do:** Monitor DPD (days past due) buckets, classify accounts into SMA-0/1/2 and NPA stages, compute provisions under Ind AS 109 (ECL), prepare regulatory returns for RBI on asset quality, and feed the capital adequacy computation
- **Pain:** Data comes from the loan management system (LMS) and core banking, often with a 1-2 day lag. Staging is done in Excel or a bespoke system. When a borrower also has fraud signals, the credit team usually does not know ΓÇö different system, different team.

**4. Treasury / ALM (Liquidity Risk)**
- **People:** Treasury middle office, ALM desk, CFO's office
- **What they do:** Bucket assets and liabilities by maturity, compute LCR and structural liquidity gaps, report to ALCO (Asset-Liability Committee) and RBI
- **Pain:** Behavioural assumptions (e.g., what fraction of demand deposits actually leave in 30 days) are governance objects maintained in spreadsheets. The computation itself is often Excel-based even at mid-size NBFCs.

---

## The data sources they use today

| Source | What it provides | Current state |
|---|---|---|
| **Core Banking System (CBS)** | Account balances, customer master, transaction history | Usually Oracle/Finacle/T24. Data extracted via overnight batch ETL into a data warehouse or directly queried. |
| **Loan Management System (LMS)** | Loan disbursements, repayment schedules, DPD, collateral | Often a separate system from CBS. Credit team pulls reports manually or via scheduled extracts. |
| **Transaction Monitoring System (TMS)** | Alerts on rule-based thresholds (velocity, amount, geography) | Products like Actimize, Mantas, SAS AML. Generates alerts; investigation happens in a separate case management tool. |
| **KYC/CDD platform** | Customer due diligence records, PEP screening results, risk ratings | Often partially manual ΓÇö paper documents scanned, verified by operations staff. |
| **Sanctions screening tool** | Real-time screening against OFAC, UN, EU, MHA lists | Usually a vendor product (Fircosoft, Accuity). Runs at payment initiation and periodically against the customer base. |
| **Case management system** | Investigation workflow, evidence attachments, disposition | Sometimes a vendor tool, sometimes Jira/ServiceNow, sometimes literally email and shared drives. |
| **Excel** | Everything the systems above do not cover | This is not a joke. Provisioning models, ALM bucketing, regulatory return templates, reconciliation ΓÇö a huge fraction lives in analyst-maintained spreadsheets. |
| **Regulatory circulars / Master Directions** | Policy text, thresholds, reporting formats | PDFs on the RBI website. A compliance officer reads them, interprets them, and manually updates internal policy documents and system rules. |
| **Sanctions/PEP lists** | OFAC SDN, UN Consolidated List, MHA UAPA | XML/CSV files downloaded periodically, loaded into the screening tool. |

---

## The workflow being replaced

The core pain is not any single step ΓÇö it is the **manual stitching across systems**. Here is a concrete example of the current workflow for an AML investigation:

```
1. TMS fires an alert: "Account X received 12 credits from 8 different 
   accounts totalling Γé╣47L in 3 days, all just under Γé╣10L each"

2. L1 analyst opens the alert in the case management tool. Sees the 
   alert summary but no context.

3. Analyst logs into CBS, pulls transaction history for Account X. 
   Copies into Excel.

4. Analyst logs into KYC platform, pulls customer profile. Notes: 
   salaried individual, low-risk rated, no PEP flags.

5. Analyst manually checks the 8 source accounts ΓÇö are any of them 
   also customers? Logs into CBS again, searches one by one.

6. Finds 3 are customers. Pulls their profiles. Notices two share a 
   phone number with Account X. This is not flagged anywhere ΓÇö the 
   analyst spotted it by reading.

7. Analyst escalates to L2. L2 investigator repeats much of the same 
   work, plus runs the source accounts through sanctions screening 
   manually.

8. Investigator decides this warrants an STR. Opens a Word template. 
   Begins writing the narrative: who, what accounts, what pattern, 
   what period, what amount, why suspicious, what evidence.

9. Every number in the narrative is manually copied from the Excel 
   extracts. No automated cross-check.

10. Draft goes to MLRO for review. MLRO asks for the fund-flow 
    diagram. Investigator builds it manually in PowerPoint.

11. MLRO sends back with comments. Two revision cycles over 3 days.

12. MLRO signs off. STR is filed with FIU-IND.

13. Meanwhile, the credit team has no idea this happened. Account X 
    is also a borrower with Γé╣15L outstanding. The fraud signal never 
    reaches the credit risk dashboard.
```

**Steps 3-6 are pure data gathering across siloed systems.** Steps 8-11 are manual narrative drafting with no automated evidence chain. Step 13 is the cross-silo blindness the plan calls "the unifying insight."

---

## What the copilot replaces, specifically

| Current state | Target state |
|---|---|
| Analyst manually pulls data from 4-6 systems | Agent queries one semantic layer; evidence is gathered and frozen with point-in-time references |
| Shared-device/phone link spotted by reading | Graph query over `PartyRelationship` surfaces the ring automatically |
| STR narrative written in Word from memory and Excel | Agent drafts cited narrative; every number traces to a query result; reviewer agent validates before human sees it |
| MLRO reviews a Word doc with no provenance | MLRO reviews a finding with linked evidence, each piece re-verifiable via Time Travel |
| Credit team unaware of fraud signals on their borrower | Same `party_id` surfaces the fraud signal in the credit exposure view |
| Policy threshold changes require a developer to update system rules | New circular is parsed into structured clauses, diffed against current rules, impact-assessed, and queued for human approval |
| Regulatory returns assembled in Excel | Verified queries produce deterministic numbers; the agent assembles the return and cites the computation |

The target audience is not the CTO ΓÇö it is the **MLRO, the head of fraud operations, and the CRO's office**. People who sign things and face regulators. The system earns their trust by making the evidence chain visible and re-verifiable, not by being fast or clever.

Let me map this precisely against the PS requirements. I will go role by role, process by process, with no speculation ΓÇö only what the PS explicitly asks for and what the domain requires.

---

## The PS, decomposed into functional requirements

The PS contains five distinct technical demands. Everything below maps back to these:

| # | PS text | What it actually requires |
|---|---|---|
| **R1** | "Combine transaction and account data with policy and filing text" | A joined data layer: structured (transactions, accounts, exposures) + unstructured (policy docs, circulars, filing templates) |
| **R2** | "Let a business or compliance user ask questions" | Natural language interface for non-technical users |
| **R3** | "Get governed, explainable, evidence-backed answers" | Every answer cites its source data, the rule that applies, and the query that produced the number |
| **R4** | "Cover the flow from signal to evidence to a documented finding or report" | A persisted pipeline: detection ΓåÆ investigation ΓåÆ evidence gathering ΓåÆ reasoning ΓåÆ output artifact |
| **R5** | "Produces audit-ready regulatory outputs" | The final deliverable is a document a regulator would accept ΓÇö not a dashboard, not a chat answer |

---

## Target user 1: The AML Compliance Officer

**Who they are:** Mid-career compliance professional, 5-15 years experience. Reports to the MLRO (Money Laundering Reporting Officer) or Chief Compliance Officer. Not technical ΓÇö they use the systems they are given but do not write queries or code. They are legally accountable for the quality of what they file.

**Their daily reality:**

### Process A: Transaction monitoring alert triage

**Current workflow, exactly:**

```
1. Log into the TMS (Actimize, SAS, Mantas, or similar). See a queue 
   of 40-80 alerts assigned for the day.

2. Open alert #1. The TMS shows: "Account 4521XXXX received 7 inward 
   transfers totalling Γé╣6.8L from 5 distinct remitters in 48 hours. 
   Rule: RAPID_CREDIT_VELOCITY."

3. The TMS shows the transactions that fired the rule. Nothing else.

4. To investigate, the officer opens a SECOND application ΓÇö the core 
   banking system (Finacle, T24, Flexcube). Searches for the account. 
   Pulls the full transaction history for the last 90 days. Reads it 
   on screen or exports to Excel.

5. Opens a THIRD application ΓÇö the KYC/CDD platform. Pulls the 
   customer profile: occupation (salaried, Γé╣4.2L annual income), 
   risk rating (medium), KYC renewal date, source of funds declared 
   at onboarding.

6. Mentally compares: Γé╣6.8L inward in 48 hours vs Γé╣4.2L declared 
   annual income. Notes the mismatch.

7. Wants to know: who are the 5 remitters? Goes back to CBS. Searches 
   each remitter account one by one. 3 are customers of the same bank. 
   2 are external (only account numbers visible, no profile).
```

**What the copilot replaces:**

- Steps 2-4 are **R1** + **R3** ΓÇö the LCR computation is a verified query over a semantic view. Regulatory haircuts and run-off rates are policy data in `PolicyClause` with effective dates.
- Step 5 is **R5** ΓÇö the structural liquidity statement is an artifact.
- Step 6 is **R1** ΓÇö behavioural assumptions are a governed object, version-controlled and effective-dated.

---

## Data Sources ΓÇö Complete Map

| Source | What we ingest | What it replaces |
|---|---|---|
| **Core Banking System** | Transaction feed (Snowpipe Streaming for real-time, batch for history), account master, customer master | Manual CBS lookups during investigation |
| **Loan Management System** | Exposure data: outstanding, limit, DPD, repayment schedule, collateral | Manual LMS extracts into Excel |
| **KYC/CDD platform** | Customer risk rating, PEP status, CDD records, beneficial ownership | Manual KYC lookups during investigation |
| **General Ledger** | Balance sheet positions by GL code | Manual GL extracts for ALM |
| **Sanctions lists (OFAC, UN, MHA)** | Structured watchlist entries, refreshed daily | Vendor sanctions screening tool |
| **RBI circulars / Master Directions** | Policy text ΓåÆ parsed into structured `PolicyClause` records | Compliance officer manually reading PDFs and updating internal policy docs |
| **FIU-IND reporting formats** | Filing templates and field definitions | Officer manually filling Word/Excel templates |
| **Case management system** | Replaced entirely by `Case`, `Evidence`, `Finding`, `Artifact`, `Attestation` tables | Jira/ServiceNow/email/shared drives |

**What we do NOT ingest** (explicit):
- Credit bureau data (commercial, licensed ΓÇö note as integration point)
- Real customer data (entire dataset is synthetic ΓÇö a strength, not a gap)
- Payment network data (NPCI/SWIFT raw feeds ΓÇö simulated)

---

## Summary: The Replacement Map

| PS requirement | Current process | Current pain | What the copilot delivers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R1** "Combine transaction and account data with policy and filing text" | Officer logs into 4-6 systems, manually cross-references | 70-80% of investigation time is data gathering | One semantic layer joining structured data with parsed policy rules |
| **R2** "Let a business or compliance user ask questions" | Officer writes no queries; relies on canned reports and manual lookups | Cannot ask ad-hoc questions without IT support | Natural language over verified queries ΓÇö deterministic answers from governed SQL |
| **R3** "Governed, explainable, evidence-backed answers" | Numbers are manually transcribed; no provenance chain | "Where did this number come from?" is unanswerable after the fact | Every answer cites query ID, source rows, as-of timestamp, and applicable policy clause |
| **R4** "Signal to evidence to documented finding" | Alert ΓåÆ manual investigation ΓåÆ Word document with no data lineage | The chain exists only in the officer's memory and their Excel files | Persisted pipeline: Signal ΓåÆ Case ΓåÆ Evidence ΓåÆ Finding ΓåÆ Artifact ΓåÆ Attestation |
| **R5** "Audit-ready regulatory outputs" | Officer manually assembles returns in Excel/Word; MLRO reviews prose with no automated cross-check | Revision cycles, transcription errors, stale policy references, no reproducibility | Agent-drafted artifacts with numeric reconciliation gate; every number re-verifiable via Time Travel |

**Key insight:** The users are not looking for a faster dashboard. They are looking to stop spending 80% of their time gathering data and transcribing numbers, so they can spend that time on the judgement calls they are actually paid and legally accountable for.

content.displayText: So, do we progress with AML and Fraud Detection first? Explain how the current day core banking software platforms and TMS are not providing this bridge with each other if it's a well known wide spread problem. If we can dwelve into this space at all, is it non existent in the current day. In depth, reasons/findings backed reasoning awaited

content.text:
This is a critical question. Before we commit to scope, you are right to pressure-test whether we are solving a real gap or building something that already exists. Let me be precise and honest.

---

## The short answer

Yes, the bridge between fraud/AML and credit/liquidity is genuinely broken in current-day banking infrastructure. It is not broken because nobody noticed ΓÇö it is broken because of how these systems were built, sold, procured, regulated, and organisationally owned over the last 30 years. The gap is structural, not accidental, and it persists even at large, well-resourced banks.

But the gap is not total. There are partial solutions emerging. I will be specific about what exists, what does not, and where our copilot sits relative to the current state.

---

## Why core banking systems do not bridge this

### The architecture of a CBS

A core banking system (Finacle, T24, Flexcube, BaNCS) is a **transaction processing engine**. Its design priorities, in order, are:

1. **ACID correctness** ΓÇö every debit has a credit, every balance is consistent, every posting is recoverable
2. **Throughput** ΓÇö process millions of transactions per day with sub-second latency
3. **Regulatory accounting** ΓÇö GL postings, interest accrual, tax withholding, regulatory returns on balances and positions

A CBS is optimised to answer: **"What is the current state of this account?"** It is not optimised to answer: "Is the pattern of activity on this account suspicious?" or "Does this customer's behaviour across all their accounts and relationships resemble a known fraud typology?"

**Specific architectural constraints:**

- **Account-centric, not party-centric.** The primary key in a CBS is the account number. A customer who holds 3 accounts (savings, current, loan) is three separate rows in most operational views. The "customer master" exists but is a reference table, not the spine the system is built on. Joining across a customer's accounts for behavioural analysis requires cross-account queries that the CBS was not designed to serve at scale or in real time.

- **No graph model.** A CBS stores relationships as flat attributes (joint holder, guarantor, power of attorney). It does not store or traverse **networks** ΓÇö "Account A sent money to Account B, which shares a phone number with Account C, which is owned by a director of Company D." That traversal requires a graph query. The CBS data model has no edges and no traversal engine.

- **No behavioural history in queryable form.** A CBS stores transactions. It does not store derived behavioural features: 30-day velocity, channel entropy, counterparty concentration, time-of-day distribution, deviation from historical pattern. These features must be computed externally and stored elsewhere. The CBS has no facility to define, compute, or serve them.

- **No unstructured data capability.** Policy documents, circulars, KYC narratives, complaint text, prior STR filings ΓÇö none of this lives in the CBS. The CBS deals in numbers and codes, not in text that needs to be parsed, matched, or cited.

### Why the CBS vendors have not fixed this

It is not in their interest to. The CBS is a **mission-critical system** ΓÇö the one system that, if it goes down, the bank cannot operate. Every CBS vendor's first priority is stability and regulatory compliance on the accounting side. Adding analytical, behavioural, or graph capabilities to the CBS would increase its attack surface, its resource consumption, and its failure modes ΓÇö all unacceptable to the operations team that owns it.

The CBS vendors' response to the analytics gap has been to build **separate products** (Infosys had iCashPro, Oracle built FCCM, Temenos has Financial Crime Mitigation) and sell them alongside the CBS. But these are separate systems with separate data stores, which brings us to the next problem.

---

## Why Transaction Monitoring Systems do not bridge this

### What a TMS actually is

A TMS (Actimize NICE, SAS Anti-Money Laundering, Oracle FCCM, Mantas, Norkom, Fircosoft) is a **rule engine with a data warehouse underneath it**. Its architecture:

1. **ETL from CBS** ΓÇö nightly or intra-day batch extract of transactions, accounts, and customer records from the CBS into the TMS's own data store
2. **Feature computation** ΓÇö calculate derived features (velocity, volume, counterparty counts, deviation from peer group) over the extracted data
3. **Rule execution** ΓÇö run detection rules/scenarios against the features. Output: alerts.
4. **Alert management** ΓÇö queue alerts for analyst review, track dispositions, manage cases

### The specific gaps

**Gap 1: The TMS sees transactions, not the full picture.**

The TMS ingests what the CBS gives it ΓÇö transaction records, account attributes, basic customer demographics. It typically does **not** ingest:

- **KYC/CDD records** ΓÇö these live in a separate platform (LexisNexis, Refinitiv World-Check, or a bespoke onboarding system). The TMS may receive a risk rating (high/medium/low) but not the underlying CDD documents, beneficial ownership structure, or source-of-funds declarations.
- **Loan/exposure data** ΓÇö the LMS is a separate system. The TMS does not know that the account it flagged for suspicious inflows belongs to a borrower who is 60 DPD on a Γé╣15L loan. That is credit risk data, and credit risk is somebody else's problem.
- **Device/digital channel data** ΓÇö IP addresses, device fingerprints, session behaviour, login anomalies. These live in the digital banking platform or a separate fraud detection system (often a different product from the AML TMS, even within the same vendor's suite).
- **Unstructured investigation history** ΓÇö prior case notes, previous STR narratives, compliance committee minutes about this customer. These live in the case management system or in email.

**The TMS is a consumer of pre-curated feeds, not an integrator of raw sources.** It sees what its ETL was configured to extract, and that configuration was set during implementation (often years ago) and rarely expanded because every new feed requires schema changes, testing, and re-validation.

**Gap 2: Fraud and AML are often separate TMS instances.**

This is the one that surprises people outside banking.

At many institutions, fraud detection and AML detection are **separate systems**, often from **separate vendors**, managed by **separate teams**, with **separate data feeds**:

- **Fraud** is real-time, transaction-level, owned by the fraud operations team (often under the COO or head of operations). It focuses on: is this specific transaction fraudulent? Respond in milliseconds to block/allow.
- **AML** is batch, entity-level, owned by the compliance team (under the CCO or MLRO). It focuses on: has this customer's overall pattern of activity over weeks/months been suspicious?

These two systems often cannot talk to each other directly. A fraud alert on a transaction does not automatically become an AML signal on the customer. The handoff, when it happens, is **manual** ΓÇö a fraud investigator who suspects money laundering escalates via email or a case note to the compliance team, who then opens a separate investigation in a separate system.

**Why this persists:** Procurement. Fraud and AML are separate budget lines, approved by separate committees, with separate vendor selection processes. The fraud system was bought in 2015 from Vendor A. The AML system was bought in 2018 from Vendor B. They have incompatible data models, different alert schemas, and different case management workflows. Integrating them is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar programme that competes for budget with regulatory mandates and core system upgrades.

**Gap 3: The TMS has no concept of credit risk or liquidity.**

This is the deepest gap. A TMS is a **financial crime** system. Its entire domain model is: transactions, alerts, cases, SARs/STRs. It has no concept of:

- DPD, SMA staging, NPA classification
- Provisioning or expected credit loss
- Balance sheet positions, maturity buckets, or LCR
- Capital adequacy or risk-weighted assets

These are **different regulatory regimes** (AML is PMLA/FATF; credit risk is Basel/RBI prudential norms; liquidity is Basel III LCR/NSFR), enforced by **different regulators or different departments within the same regulator**, and managed by **different teams within the bank**.

The consequence: when a fraud/AML investigation reveals that a borrower is part of a mule ring, the credit risk team is not automatically notified. The exposure continues to be classified based on DPD alone, without the fraud signal. The capital computation does not reflect the increased risk. This is not a theoretical problem ΓÇö it is the exact scenario that causes banks to discover, after the fact, that they were under-provisioned on a portfolio that had both credit deterioration and fraud.

---

## What exists today that partially addresses this

I will not pretend the industry has done nothing. Here is what exists, honestly assessed.

### Enterprise data warehouses / data lakes

Most mid-to-large banks have built a central data warehouse (often on Oracle, Teradata, or more recently on cloud platforms like Snowflake or Databricks) that ingests from multiple source systems. This partially addresses the data silo problem ΓÇö the data is in one place.

**But:** The warehouse is a **repository**, not an **intelligence layer**. It stores the data; it does not join it for investigative purposes, does not run detection logic, does not produce evidence chains, and does not generate regulatory artifacts. The analyst still has to know which tables to query, how to join them, and how to interpret the results. A warehouse without a semantic layer and without an agent layer is just a bigger cabinet to search through.

### Vendor "platforms" that claim end-to-end coverage

The major vendors now offer suites that nominally cover fraud, AML, and "enterprise risk":

- **NICE Actimize** ΓÇö X-Sight platform, claims to unify fraud, AML, and compliance
- **SAS** ΓÇö has fraud, AML, and risk management products
- **Oracle** ΓÇö FCCM covers fraud and AML; separate products for credit and market risk
- **Refinitiv (LSEG)** ΓÇö World-Check for screening, enhanced due diligence products

**The reality:**

- These are **suites of separate products** marketed under a unified brand, not truly integrated systems. Actimize's fraud product and AML product share a brand name but often have different data models, different UIs, different databases, and different implementation timelines. "Unified" means they can be sold together and share some reference data, not that a fraud signal automatically enriches an AML case or that either connects to credit risk.
- **No vendor covers all four pillars.** Fraud and AML are the closest to integrated (same vendor, at least). Credit risk and liquidity risk are entirely separate products from separate vendors (Moody's, S&P, internal models). Nobody sells a product that takes a fraud signal and traces it through to its impact on CRAR.
- **Licensing costs are prohibitive for mid-size institutions.** An NBFC with Γé╣10,000 Cr AUM is not buying the full Actimize suite. They are running a basic TMS, a basic CBS, and a lot of Excel. This is the segment where the gap is widest and where a Snowflake-native solution has the most room.

### RegTech startups

A newer wave of companies (Tookitaki, Lucinity, Napier AI, Hawk AI, and Indian players like CashFlo, SignDesk) offer AI-augmented AML or fraud solutions, often cloud-native.

**What they get right:** Better UX than legacy TMS, some use graph analytics for network detection, some use NLP for STR drafting assistance.

**What they do not do:**

- None of them bridge to credit risk or liquidity. They are financial-crime-only.
- None of them produce the full evidence chain with point-in-time reproducibility. They improve the investigation workflow but still output documents, not re-verifiable evidence bundles.
- None of them ingest and structure policy text as effective-dated rules. They may RAG over policy docs, but that is the weak version (see SOLUTION-PLAN ┬º3.3).
- None of them run inside the customer's data platform. They are SaaS products that require data to be shipped out to the vendor's environment ΓÇö a non-starter for many regulated institutions.

---

## Where our copilot sits ΓÇö the actual gap

The gap is not "nobody does fraud detection" or "nobody does AML." The gap is precise and specific:

### Gap A: The cross-domain join on a single entity

No current product takes a `party_id` and returns: here are their transaction alerts (fraud), their AML case history, their credit exposure and staging, and their contribution to the institution's regulatory capital ΓÇö in one view, from one query, over one governed data layer.

This is the "one entity, four lenses" demo spine from the solution plan, and it is genuinely non-existent in current tooling because the four domains have separate vendors, separate teams, separate data models, and separate regulatory mandates. Nobody has commercial incentive to build the bridge because each vendor owns one pillar and does not want to depend on another vendor's data.

### Gap B: The evidence chain as a data object

Current tools produce **documents** ΓÇö PDFs, Word files, Excel exports. The STR is a Word document. The provisioning report is an Excel file. The LCR statement is a PDF. Once produced, the link between the document and the underlying data is broken. You cannot click a number in the STR and see the query that produced it, re-executed at the same timestamp.

This is not a feature limitation ΓÇö it is an architectural limitation. Document-based outputs cannot carry re-executable provenance. Only a system where the evidence, the finding, and the artifact are **database objects with foreign keys to the source data** can support this. That is what our `Evidence`-as-pointers model provides.

### Gap C: Policy-as-structured-data with change management

No current product ingests regulatory circulars, parses them into structured effective-dated rules, diffs them against current controls, and reports impact. The closest is GRC (Governance, Risk, and Compliance) software like MetricStream or Archer, which tracks policy documents and control mappings ΓÇö but as manually maintained metadata, not as automatically extracted, effective-dated, queryable data.

The regulatory change management feature (SOLUTION-PLAN ┬º7.2) addresses a pain point that every compliance officer experiences and no current tool solves: "A new RBI circular just came out. Which of my controls does it affect? Which of my open findings relied on the threshold that just changed?"

### Gap D: Deterministic computation with natural language access

Current BI tools (Power BI, Tableau, Looker) offer natural language query, but over whatever data model exists ΓÇö which for regulatory metrics means either (a) the analyst pre-built the exact dashboard, or (b) the NL engine generates SQL that may or may not compute the metric correctly.

The semantic view + verified query approach guarantees that "what is our current LCR?" always produces the same deterministic SQL, regardless of how the question is phrased. The NL interface is not over raw tables ΓÇö it is over a curated semantic layer where every regulatory metric has exactly one verified computation. This is what "governed" means in the PS.

---

## Recommendation: proceed with Fraud + AML as primary, credit as bridge

The reasoning:

1. **Fraud + AML share the transaction spine.** Building one makes the second nearly free in data terms. They share `Party`, `Account`, `Transaction`, `PartyRelationship`. The marginal cost of AML detection after fraud detection is the AML-specific rules and the STR artifact ΓÇö not a new data model.

2. **The STR is the best artifact to demonstrate.** It is narrative, evidence-backed, regulatorily mandated, genuinely hand-written today, and the single most time-consuming output a compliance officer produces. Generating a cited, reconciliation-checked STR from a natural language request is the most compelling demo of R5.

3. **The cross-silo bridge is the differentiator, not the detection.** Fraud detection alone is a TMS ΓÇö we are not building a better TMS. The value is: fraud signal surfaces in the AML investigation, the AML investigation surfaces in the credit exposure view, and the credit exposure flows into the capital computation. That chain is what no current product provides. Credit risk (SMA staging, provisioning) is the cheapest way to demonstrate the bridge ΓÇö it requires only exposure data and a set of deterministic rules.

4. **Liquidity (LCR) is the fourth lens if time permits.** It is architecturally independent (balance sheet data, not transaction data), so it does not block the other three. It proves the balance-sheet regulatory axis. But if scope is tight, the first three pillars (fraud, AML, credit) already demonstrate cross-domain joins and all five PS requirements.

The answer to your question ΓÇö "is this gap non-existent in current day?" ΓÇö is: **the individual pillars are served by existing products; the bridge between them is genuinely non-existent in any commercially available tool.** That bridge is our product. Fraud + AML first, credit as the bridge, liquidity if time allows.

Snowpipe Streaming
Snowpipe Streaming is SnowflakeΓÇÖs real-time ingestion service built on our latest high-performance architecture. It enables applications to stream rows directly from devices, applications, and services into Snowflake tables or Snowflake-managed Apache Iceberg tables. This direct path can remove staging files, intermediate object storage, message buses, and connector services that the workload doesnΓÇÖt otherwise need.
Snowpipe Streaming supports two ingestion modes. In both modes, a channel is a logical path that carries rows through a pipe to a target table:

Elastic Channels are the recommended starting point for most new applications. Producers write directly without creating or coordinating channels; Snowflake manages them and scales ingestion as traffic changes. An acknowledgement confirms that Snowflake has durably buffered the append, so the producer can release its retained copy; table processing and query visibility follow. Elastic Channels provide at-least-once delivery without an ordering guarantee. Producers retain unacknowledged events according to their delivery requirements.
Named Channels provide ordered, exactly-once ingestion within each channel by using offset tokens. Use Named Channels when reading from a source that requires strict ordering semantics, such as Kafka partitions or Change Data Capture (CDC).

Snowpipe Streaming delivers:

Up to 20 GB/s throughput per table
As low as 5 seconds ingest-to-queryable latency
Direct ingestion without application-managed channels through Elastic Channels
Ordered, exactly-once ingestion through Named Channels and offset tokens
Streaming into Snowflake-managed Apache Iceberg tables

The results you observe depend on workload shape and configuration, including row size, table width (number of columns), SDK buffering or REST request batching, concurrency, table type, transformations, and clustering.
Why use Snowpipe Streaming
Simpler direct ingestion: Elastic Channels let producers stream rows directly from devices and services into Snowflake, reducing pipeline hops without requiring you to create channels or coordinate ingestion across producers. Snowflake scales the ingest path as producers and traffic change.
Exactly-once and ordered ingestion when required: Named Channels use offset tokens to track committed progress and preserve row order within each channel. They map naturally to source partitions and make strict exactly-once recovery straightforward.
High throughput, low latency: Designed to support ingest speeds of up to 20 GB/s per table, with ingest-to-queryable latency as low as 5 seconds. Results depend on workload shape and configuration.
In-flight transformations: Cleanse, reshape, and transform data during ingestion by using COPY command syntax within the PIPE object. Reorder columns, cast types, and apply expressions before data is committed to the target table, with no separate ETL step needed.
Pre-clustering at ingest time: Sort data during ingestion for optimized query performance on tables with clustering keys.
Apache Iceberg table support: Stream data into Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables, including both Iceberg v2 and Iceberg v3 tables. For more information, see Snowpipe Streaming high-performance architecture with Apache IcebergΓäó tables.
Schema evolution: Automatically adapt table schemas to changing data structures. Snowflake can add new columns detected in the incoming stream without manual DDL changes.
Row-level error visibility: Enable error logging to capture rows that fail processing after acknowledgement, with details for diagnosis and recovery.
Simplified pipelines: With Elastic Channels, producers write rows directly into Snowflake tables or Iceberg tables without staging files or intermediate message-bus infrastructure that the workload doesnΓÇÖt otherwise need.
Serverless and scalable: Compute resources scale automatically based on ingestion load. No infrastructure to manage.
Transparent pricing: Throughput-based billing calculated by credits per uncompressed GB of data ingested. For more information, see Snowpipe Streaming high-performance architecture: Understand your costs.

How to connect
Snowpipe Streaming supports multiple ingestion paths to fit different workloads:

The Java, Python, and Node.js SDKs use a shared Rust-based client core. Append rows as they arrive: the SDK automatically buffers and batches appends using time and size thresholds, and handles compression and sending data to Snowflake. Direct REST clients instead group rows into newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON), with one JSON object per line, and handle compression themselves.
NoteWhere possible, use the Snowpipe Streaming SDK instead of the REST API to benefit from automatic batching and simpler integration. Use direct REST when an SDK isnΓÇÖt suitable for your environment.
To get started, choose Elastic Channels or Named Channels, then follow the SDK or REST tutorial in that section.
For a side-by-side comparison and use-case guidance, see Choosing a channel type.
For technical details about the PIPE object, channels, offset tokens, and supported data types, see Key concepts.
Recommended for
High-volume streaming workloads with per-table throughput needs of up to 20 GB/s

Snowpipe Streaming versus Snowpipe
Snowpipe Streaming and Snowpipe complement each other. Use Snowpipe Streaming when data arrives as rows from applications, devices, or services and you need low-latency data availability. Use Snowpipe when your pipeline already produces files in cloud storage and batch-oriented, higher-latency loading is acceptable.

Sep 23, 2025: Snowpipe Streaming with high-performance architecture (General availability)
The high-performance architecture for Snowpipe Streaming is now generally available for all accounts on AWS. This new architecture is designed from the ground up for large-scale, real-time data ingestion with high throughput and low latency.
Key features and benefits
High performance and low latency: Ingest data at up to 10 GB per second per table, with ingest-to-query latencies typically under 10 seconds.
Multi-language client support: Use the new, high-performance Java and Python SDKs, built on a shared Rust core for efficiency. A REST API is also available for lightweight and serverless ingestion workloads.
Simplified data pipelines: Centralize your ingestion logic using the PIPE object. The new architecture moves schema validation to the server side and supports in-flight data transformations using familiar COPY command syntax, reducing client-side complexity.
Improved cost-efficiency: Benefit from a new throughput-based pricing model that provides predictable costs.
Key difference from classic architecture
This new architecture requires the use of the new SDKs or REST API. All ingestion configuration, including transformations and schema validation, is now managed through the server-side PIPE object, which acts as the entry point for all streaming data into a table.
Recommended use cases
This architecture is recommended for consistent, high-volume streaming workloads, such as powering real-time analytics dashboards, log and event analysis, and integrating data from IoT devices.
For more information, see Snowpipe Streaming: High-Performance Architecture.
