Snowpipe Streaming REST API endpoints
NoteWhere possible, use the Snowpipe Streaming SDK instead of the REST API to benefit from automatic batching and simpler integration. Use direct REST when an SDK isnΓÇÖt suitable for your environment.
The Snowpipe Streaming REST API is designed for lightweight workloads and provides a flexible way to integrate with external applications without using a Snowpipe Streaming SDK.
This reference documents both ingestion modes:

Elastic Channel endpoints for at-least-once ingestion without channel lifecycle or offset-token management.
Named Channel endpoints for ordered, exactly-once ingestion.


Request headers
The following request headers apply to all the endpoints for the Snowpipe Streaming REST API:
HeaderDescriptionAuthorizationAuthentication tokenX-Snowflake-Authorization-Token-Type (optional)JWT/OAuthContent-Encoding (optional)Specifies the compression format of the payload. Supported: gzip, zstd.User-Agent (optional)Identifies the client application. Recommended format: SnowpipeStreamingSDK/{version} ({platform}) {LANGUAGE}/{language_version} (app={partner-name}). Example: SnowpipeStreamingSDK/1.0.0 (Linux amd64) PYTHON/3.11.0 (app=MyPartnerApp).ExpandShow lessSee more
Direct REST clients must group rows into newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON), with one JSON object per line, and handle compression themselves. Both Elastic and Named Channel append requests have a 4 MB payload limit (the payload size sent over the network, after compression if used). Batch rows and use ZSTD or Gzip compression to reduce request overhead; bound batch size and elapsed time before sending.
Get Hostname
The Get Hostname returns the hostname used to interact with the Snowpipe Streaming REST API. Each account has a unique hostname.
NoteFor private connectivity (AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link, or Google Cloud Private Service Connect), call this endpoint through your private account URL, and configure private DNS for the returned ingest hostname before you use it for the scoped-token exchange and streaming operations. For complete steps, see Discover and configure the ingest host in the REST API tutorial.
GET /v2/streaming/hostname

}

The Exchange Scoped Token returns a security token that can be used to access only the Snowpipe Streaming API-related service. This provides security protection for the customer.

Elastic Channel endpoints
Elastic Channels donΓÇÖt require a separate open-channel operation. Send a batch of NDJSON rows directly to a table or to the implicit ELASTIC channel of a pipe:
POST /v2/streaming/data/databases/{databaseName}/schemas/{schemaName}/tables/{tableName}/rows
POST /v2/streaming/data/databases/{databaseName}/schemas/{schemaName}/pipes/{pipeName}/channels/ELASTIC/rows

The table endpoint is only for Elastic Channels. On the first request, Snowflake creates or resolves the managed default pipe named <tableName>-STREAMING. Each streaming pipe includes an implicit ELASTIC channel, which the request uses without a separate open-channel operation. Use the pipe endpoint for an Elastic Channel on a custom pipe with in-flight transformations or pre-clustering.
Elastic request attributes
AttributeRequiredComponentDescriptiondatabaseNameYesURIDatabase name, case-insensitive.schemaNameYesURISchema name, case-insensitive.tableName or pipeNameYesURIThe target table for the default pipe, or the custom pipe name.rowsYesBodyNDJSON rows. The maximum Elastic request payload is 4 MB (the payload size sent over the network, after compression if used).requestIdNoQuery parameterA UUID that tracks the request. Use the same value on every retry of the same rowset (batch of rows), and generate a new UUID for each distinct rowset.retryCountNoQuery parameterThe retry attempt number, starting at 0. Increment it for each retry. A value greater than 0 signals that duplicate rows are possible; it doesnΓÇÖt prove that a duplicate occurred.ExpandShow lessSee more
Elastic requests must not include offsetToken, startOffsetToken, endOffsetToken, or continuationToken.
Elastic response and delivery semantics
A successful HTTP 200 response is the durable acknowledgement: Snowflake has durably buffered the request payload. It doesnΓÇÖt mean that rows are immediately queryable in the target table. Row-level processing errors are persisted to the error table when error logging is enabled.
Copy code{
  "message": "OK"
}

Elastic Channels provide at-least-once delivery without an ordering guarantee. Retrying after an ambiguous response can produce duplicate rows. Include a stable event identifier in the row payload and reconcile or deduplicate downstream when duplicates matter.
Elastic append example
Copy codeexport REQUEST_ID=$(uuidgen)

curl -sS -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCOPED_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-ndjson" \
  "https://${INGEST_HOST}/v2/streaming/data/databases/$DB/schemas/$SCHEMA/tables/$TABLE/rows?requestId=$REQUEST_ID&retryCount=0" \
  --data-binary @rows.ndjson | jq .

For a retry of this rowset, reuse REQUEST_ID and increment retryCount. To use a custom pipe, replace the table path with /pipes/$PIPE/channels/ELASTIC/rows.

1. Use streams on dynamic tables
   URL: https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/dynamic-tables/streams-on-dts

   Source: Primary Documentation
   Content:
Use streams on dynamic tables
A stream on a dynamic table captures row-level inserts, updates, and
deletes. Each read returns the net changes since the previous read. This lets you bridge a dynamic table pipeline into targets that
dynamic tables canΓÇÖt reach on their own, such as stored procedures, external API calls, or
conditional logic in a task.
This example assumes you have an existing dynamic table named dt_orders that uses an incremental
refresh. See Create a dynamic table for setup guidance.
ImportantUse the ON DYNAMIC TABLE syntax when creating the stream. ON TABLE doesnΓÇÖt work with dynamic
tables and returns an error. See Common error for an
example.
Copy codeCREATE OR REPLACE STREAM dt_orders_stream ON DYNAMIC TABLE dt_orders;


Supported stream types
Streams on dynamic tables support only the standard (delta) type. The standard stream captures
inserts, updates, and deletes as net changes since the stream was last read.
Copy codeCREATE STREAM ... ON DYNAMIC TABLE <name>

APPEND_ONLY is not supported for streams on dynamic tables. If you need
insert-only semantics, consume the standard stream and filter on METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' in
your downstream task. Alternatively, custom incremental dynamic tables
support append-only semantics natively through the CHANGES(INFORMATION => APPEND_ONLY) clause.
NoteThe dynamic table must use an incremental refresh. Dynamic tables that use a full refresh donΓÇÖt
support streams because each refresh replaces the entire table output, so there is no incremental
change history to track. If REFRESH_MODE is set to AUTO, verify the resolved mode by running
SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES and checking the refresh_mode column before creating a stream.

When to use this pattern
The primary use case is a hybrid pipeline where a dynamic table handles the declarative definition
and a triggered task handles imperative work the dynamic table canΓÇÖt express:
Dynamic table -> stream -> triggered task -> target
Common scenarios:

Writing to a non-dynamic-table target (regular table, external stage).
Calling a stored procedure or external function with side effects.
Running conditional logic (IF/ELSE, loops) on the change set.

Use SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA in the taskΓÇÖs WHEN clause so the task fires only when the stream has
unconsumed changes. The task runs after the dynamic table refreshes and produces new output. A
refresh that changes no rows doesnΓÇÖt trigger the task.
Copy code-- Create a triggered task that consumes the stream
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK load_completed_orders
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('dt_orders_stream')
AS
  INSERT INTO completed_orders_archive
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, product_name, line_total
  FROM dt_orders_stream
  WHERE order_status = 'completed';

If multiple tasks consume the same dynamic table, create a separate stream for each. See Introduction to streams for details.

Stream behavior after reinitialization
When a dynamic table reinitializes (for example,
after a CREATE OR REPLACE on a base table, a masking policy change, or a change-tracking toggle),
the stream survives but its next read can return a much larger set of change rows than a normal
refresh produces. The stream remains attached and exposes all row-level differences between its last-read offset and the reinitialized output.
WarningAfter reinitialization, rows that were previously updates will appear as DELETE + INSERT pairs with
METADATA$ISUPDATE set to FALSE. Downstream logic that relies on METADATA$ISUPDATE to distinguish
real deletes from updates can lose or duplicate data without an error. Use idempotent MERGE statements
rather than conditional INSERT/DELETE branching to handle this safely.
The following MERGE handles both normal changes and the DELETE + INSERT pairs that appear after
reinitialization. The three clauses cover deletes, updates, and inserts by matching on the primary
key:
Copy codeMERGE INTO completed_orders_archive t
USING (
    SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, product_name, line_total,
           METADATA$ACTION,
           METADATA$ISUPDATE
    FROM dt_orders_stream
    WHERE order_status = 'completed'
) s ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED
    AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'DELETE'
    AND NOT s.METADATA$ISUPDATE THEN
    DELETE
WHEN MATCHED
    AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN
    UPDATE SET t.customer_id  = s.customer_id,
               t.order_date   = s.order_date,
               t.product_name = s.product_name,
               t.line_total   = s.line_total
WHEN NOT MATCHED
    AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN
    INSERT (order_id, customer_id, order_date, product_name, line_total)
    VALUES (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.order_date, s.product_name, s.line_total);

After reinitialization, every surviving row appears as a DELETE + INSERT pair with
METADATA$ISUPDATE = FALSE. The MERGE processes each pair correctly: Clause 1 removes the old row,
Clause 3 re-inserts it. The net effect is the same data, with no duplicates or data loss. For normal
changes, Clause 2 handles updates in place.
Design your downstream task to handle these large change sets gracefully. Use idempotent inserts or
batch processing so that a post-reinitialization read doesnΓÇÖt cause duplicate or missing data.

Limitation: streams capture net changes, not full history
DonΓÇÖt use a stream on a dynamic table as an audit log. If a row is inserted and then updated within a single
refresh cycle, the stream shows only the final state. If the stream is not read between two
refreshes, the changes from both refreshes collapse into a single net result.
If you need every state transition for compliance or auditing, write directly to an append-only
table from your ingestion layer instead. See Introduction to streams for
more on how streams track changes.
Verify the stream
After creating the stream, confirm it is attached and not stale:
Copy codeSHOW STREAMS LIKE 'dt_orders_stream';

+--------------------+---------------+---------------+--------------+-------+-------+
| name               | database_name | schema_name   | source_type  | mode  | stale |
|--------------------+---------------+---------------+--------------+-------+-------|
| DT_ORDERS_STREAM  | MY_DB         | PUBLIC        | Dynamic Table| DEFAULT| false |
+--------------------+---------------+---------------+--------------+-------+-------+

Output columns are truncated for readability. Check the stale column to confirm the stream is
active. If stale shows true, the stream has fallen behind the dynamic tableΓÇÖs change history
and must be recreated. To prevent staleness, make sure the stream is read regularly within the data
retention period. See Introduction to streams for details on stream
staleness.

Common error
Using ON TABLE instead of ON DYNAMIC TABLE returns an error:
Copy code-- Incorrect: ON TABLE doesn't work with dynamic tables
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM dt_orders_stream ON TABLE dt_orders;

002203 (42601): SQL compilation error:
Object found is of type 'DYNAMIC_TABLE', not specified type 'TABLE'.

To create a stream on a dynamic table, use the ON DYNAMIC TABLE syntax:
Copy code-- Correct syntax
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM dt_orders_stream ON DYNAMIC TABLE dt_orders;

Required privileges
To create a stream on a dynamic table, your role needs:

CREATE STREAM on the schema.
SELECT on the dynamic table.

For the full list of access control requirements, see CREATE STREAM.
WhatΓÇÖs next
To learn how dynamic table refreshes work, see Dynamic table refresh modes.
To monitor refresh health for the upstream dynamic table, see
Monitor dynamic tables.
To troubleshoot refresh failures that affect streams, see
Troubleshoot dynamic table refresh issues.
For the full stream SQL reference, see CREATE STREAM.

   Content:
Migrate from streams and tasks to dynamic tables
Dynamic tables replace imperative pipeline code (INSERT, MERGE, stored procedure calls) with a declarative model: you write a SELECT that describes the result you want, and Snowflake keeps it fresh.
This page covers how to convert streams-and-tasks pipelines to dynamic tables one task at a time.

Concept map: streams and tasks to dynamic tables
Streams and tasks conceptDynamic table equivalentNotesBase tableBase tableSame object, no change required.Stream on base table(built in)Snowflake tracks changes automatically. You donΓÇÖt create a separate stream.Task body (INSERT INTO ... SELECT ...)The definition in CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE ΓÇª AS SELECTWrite only the SELECT. No DML statements (such as INSERT INTO or MERGE).Task schedule (SCHEDULE = '10 MINUTE')TARGET_LAG = ΓÇÖ10 minutesΓÇÖTARGET_LAG is a freshness goal, not a fixed interval. Snowflake decides when to refresh.Task DAG (root task + child tasks)Pipeline of dynamic tablesIntermediate dynamic tables use TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM. The terminal dynamic table carries the freshness goal.Root taskTerminal dynamic table (or controller dynamic table)The terminal dynamic table drives the refresh schedule for the whole pipeline.MERGE ON key WHEN MATCHED UPDATE ΓÇªQUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1Dynamic tables express ΓÇ£latest state per keyΓÇ¥ as a window function, not as DML. See the SCD Type 1 example.SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA() check(not needed)Snowflake skips refreshes automatically when base tables havenΓÇÖt changed.ExpandShow lessSee more

Choose a migration strategy
Dynamic tables support two operational models. Choose the one that fits your teamΓÇÖs workflow.
Self-refreshing dynamic tables (Snowflake manages timing)
Set a TARGET_LAG value and Snowflake handles the refresh schedule. This is the simplest model and is suited for new pipelines or teams that want to reduce operational overhead.
Copy codeCREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE dt_orders
    TARGET_LAG = '10 minutes'
    WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
AS
    SELECT ...
    FROM raw_orders;

Best for:

New pipelines where you donΓÇÖt already have orchestration in place.
Teams that want Snowflake to manage refresh timing and dependency ordering.
Pipelines where a freshness goal (such as ΓÇ£no more than 10 minutes staleΓÇ¥) is the correct requirement.


Orchestrator-managed dynamic tables (SCHEDULER = DISABLE)
If you already run an orchestrator (dbt, Airflow, or even tasks), create dynamic tables with SCHEDULER = DISABLE. Snowflake does not schedule refreshes automatically. You trigger each refresh manually or from your orchestrator. Refreshes do not cascade upstream or downstream.
Copy code-- Create the dynamic table with scheduling disabled.
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE dt_orders
    WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
    SCHEDULER = DISABLE
AS
    SELECT ...
    FROM raw_orders;

-- Trigger a refresh manually or from your orchestrator.
ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE dt_orders REFRESH;

Key behaviors:

You canΓÇÖt set TARGET_LAG when using SCHEDULER = DISABLE.
Refreshes with SCHEDULER = DISABLE do not cascade upstream or downstream. Each dynamic table refreshes independently.
Your orchestrator controls the order, timing, and error handling.
GA since March 2026.

Best for:

Teams that want to keep their existing orchestrator while adopting declarative definitions.
Pipelines that require explicit control over refresh order or conditional refresh logic.


Decide whether to migrate a task
Evaluate each task individually against these criteria to decide whether it should migrate.
CriterionMigrate to dynamic tablesStay on streams and tasksPipeline logicPure SQL: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, CASE WHEN, window functions, custom UDFsLoops, cursors, multi-statement procedural blocksDML operationsInserts, updates, and deletes propagate from base tables through incremental refresh.Explicit DELETE, TRUNCATE, or delete-before-insert patternsData sourcesSnowflake tables, viewsExternal tables, directory tables (not supported as dynamic table inputs)Latency requirementOne minute minimum (TARGET_LAG floor). Actual freshness depends on refresh duration and pipeline depth.Sub-minute orchestration (tasks support one-second schedules)Non-deterministic functions (RANDOM)Forces FULL refresh with REFRESH_MODE = AUTO. The following patterns convert cleanly from streams and tasks to dynamic tables.

Append-only ingestion
This is the simplest migration. A stream and task that inserts new rows into a target table becomes a single

Decision guide for dynamic tables
Use this guide to choose the right approach for your data pipeline: dynamic tables, streams and tasks,
or materialized views.


Decision table
ScenarioDynamic tablesStreams and tasksMaterialized viewsSQL-based pipeline with joins or aggregationsPreferredPossibleNo (single table only)Multi-step declarative pipeline (bronze/silver/gold)PreferredPossibleNoIncremental processing of changed dataPreferred (declarative)Preferred (procedural)NoSingle-table query accelerationPossiblePossiblePreferredProcedural logic (stored procedures, IF/ELSE, loops)NoPreferredNoMERGE or complex upsert patternsNoPreferredNoExternal function calls or API integrationsNoPreferredNoAlways-current data with no lagNo (minimum TARGET_LAG setting is 1 minute)Possible (tasks run on a schedule; not zero-lag)PreferredTransparent query acceleration (optimizer rewrites queries to use the precomputed result)NoNoPreferredCustom scheduling or strict orchestration controlPossible (manual trigger only; no CRON or cascade)PreferredNoPipeline using UDFs, UDTFs, or SnowparkPossible (scalar UDFs and UDTFs with explicit column lists; Snowpark not supported)PreferredNoExpandShow lessSee more
If you need X, use Y
Use the following guidance to match your requirements to the right approach.
If you need a declarative SQL pipeline, use dynamic tables
Dynamic tables let you define the result you want as a SELECT statement. Snowflake handles refresh timing,
dependency ordering, and incremental processing. You donΓÇÖt need to write procedural code, manage streams, or
build a pipeline of tasks.
This is the recommended approach for new multi-table SQL pipelines in Snowflake, especially
pipelines with joins, aggregations, or window functions.
If you need procedural logic or custom orchestration, use streams and tasks
Streams and tasks give you full control over the pipeline logic. Use them when your pipeline needs
stored procedures, MERGE operations, external function calls, custom retry logic, or explicit scheduling
with CRON expressions. For more information, see Introduction to streams and
Introduction to tasks.
If you need single-table query acceleration, use materialized views
Materialized views accelerate repeated queries against a single base table. The query optimizer automatically
rewrites queries to use the materialized view, and the data is always current. Use materialized views when
your goal is read performance, not building a data pipeline. For more information, see
Working with Materialized Views.
Example: streams and tasks vs. dynamic tables
The following side-by-side comparison shows how the same definition (extracting names from raw JSON data)
looks with each approach. The dynamic table version replaces the stream, task, and MERGE logic with a single
SELECT statement.
Streams and tasks approach
Create a landing table.
Create a stream on the landing table.
Create a target table.
Create a task with MERGE logic to process stream records.
Resume the task.

Dynamic table approach
Create a landing table.
Create a dynamic table with the SELECT that defines the result.

Streams and tasksDynamic tablesCopy code-- Create a landing table to store
-- raw JSON data.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw
  (var VARIANT);

-- Create a stream to capture inserts
-- to the landing table.
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM rawstream1
  ON TABLE raw;

-- Create a table that stores the
-- names of office visitors from the
-- raw data.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE names
  (id INT,
   first_name STRING,
   last_name STRING);

-- Create a task that inserts new name
-- records from the rawstream1 stream
-- into the names table.
-- Run the task every minute when
-- the stream contains records.
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK raw_to_names
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  SCHEDULE = '1 minute'
  WHEN
    SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('rawstream1')
  AS
    MERGE INTO names n
      USING (
        SELECT var:id id, var:fname fname,
               var:lname lname,
               metadata$action,
               metadata$isupdate
          FROM rawstream1
      ) r1 ON n.id = TO_NUMBER(r1.id)
      WHEN MATCHED
        AND metadata$action = 'DELETE'
        AND NOT metadata$isupdate THEN
          DELETE
      WHEN MATCHED
        AND metadata$action = 'INSERT' THEN
        UPDATE SET n.first_name = r1.fname,
                   n.last_name = r1.lname
      WHEN NOT MATCHED
        AND metadata$action = 'INSERT' THEN
        INSERT (id, first_name, last_name)
          VALUES (r1.id, r1.fname, r1.lname);

-- Start the task.
ALTER TASK raw_to_names RESUME;
Copy code-- Create a landing table to store
-- raw JSON data.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw
  (var VARIANT);

-- Create a dynamic table containing
-- the names of office visitors from
-- the raw data.
-- Keep the data within 1 minute of
-- the base table.
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE dt_visitors
  TARGET_LAG = '1 minute'
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL
  AS
    SELECT
      var:id::int id,
      var:fname::string first_name,
      var:lname::string last_name
    FROM raw;

The dynamic table approach replaces four objects and MERGE logic with a single SELECT definition.
When NOT to use dynamic tables
DonΓÇÖt use dynamic tables when your pipeline has any of the following requirements. Use streams and tasks
or materialized views instead, as noted.
You need DML on the output table
Dynamic tables are read-only. You canΓÇÖt run INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE against them. If your pipeline
requires direct modifications to the output (for example, GDPR right-to-erasure requests), use streams
and tasks with a standard table.
You need stored procedures or external functions
The dynamic table definition canΓÇÖt call stored procedures, external functions, or tasks. If your pipeline
requires procedural logic, conditional branching, or external API calls, use streams and tasks.
You need sub-minute data freshness
The minimum target lag for a dynamic table is 1 minute. If you need always-current data with no lag,
use materialized views. If you need sub-minute freshness with custom logic, use streams and tasks.
You need MERGE or complex upsert patterns
Dynamic tables use a declarative model and donΓÇÖt support MERGE statements. If your pipeline relies
on upsert logic with compound keys, use streams and tasks.
You need surrogate key generation
Dynamic tables donΓÇÖt support sequence functions (SEQ1, SEQ2) or UUID_STRING in incremental
refresh mode. RANDOM() is not supported in incremental refresh mode. If you use AUTO, it resolves to FULL when the definition includes RANDOM(). If your pipeline generates surrogate keys with these functions, use streams and tasks.
Timestamp functions like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are supported in WHERE/HAVING/QUALIFY clauses. See supported queries for the full matrix.
You need schema evolution without reinitialization
Changing the definition of a dynamic table (for example, adding columns) triggers reinitialization (Snowflake reprocesses the entire table). If your pipeline requires frequent schema changes without reprocessing all data, use streams
and tasks with ALTER TABLE.
You need SCD Type 2 history tracking
Dynamic tables represent the current state of the data, not a historical record. If your pipeline
needs to track changes over time (slowly changing dimensions Type 2), use streams and tasks.
Your definition is a simple single-table query
If you only need to accelerate a query against a single base table without joins, a materialized view
is more efficient. The query optimizer automatically rewrites queries to use the materialized view, which
doesnΓÇÖt happen with dynamic tables.

Key limitations
A single account can hold a maximum of 50,000 dynamic tables.
You canΓÇÖt run DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE) on a dynamic table.
You canΓÇÖt create a temporary dynamic table.
Dynamic tables donΓÇÖt support sources that include directory tables, external tables, streams, or materialized views.
Frozen region predicates have restrictions on supported expressions. For details, see Frozen regions and backfill.
For the full list of limitations, see CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE.
WhatΓÇÖs next
After choosing your approach:

To create your first dynamic table, see Create a dynamic table.
To understand how refresh modes work, see Dynamic table refresh modes.
To set up a multi-table pipeline, see Set the target lag for a dynamic table.
For queries supported in dynamic table definitions, see Supported queries for dynamic tables.
If you chose streams and tasks, see Introduction to streams and Introduction to tasks.
If you chose materialized views, see Working with Materialized Views.

COPY INTO <table>
Loads data from files to an existing table. The files must already be in one of the following locations:


Named internal stage (or table/user stage). Files can be staged using the PUT command.


Named external stage that references an external location (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Microsoft Azure).

You cannot access data held in archival cloud storage classes that requires restoration before it can be retrieved. These archival storage classes include, for example, the Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Glacier Deep Archive storage class, or Microsoft Azure Archive Storage.


External location (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Microsoft Azure).


See also:COPY INTO <location>

Syntax
Copy code/* Standard data load */
COPY INTO [<namespace>.]<table_name>
     FROM { internalStage | externalStage | externalLocation }
[ FILES = ( '<file_name>' [ , '<file_name>' ] [ , ... ] ) ]
[ PATTERN = '<regex_pattern>' ]
[ FILE_FORMAT = ( { FORMAT_NAME = '[<namespace>.]<file_format_name>' |
                    TYPE = { CSV | JSON | AVRO | ORC | PARQUET | XML } [ formatTypeOptions ] } ) ]
[ copyOptions ]
[ VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_<n>_ROWS | RETURN_ERRORS | RETURN_ALL_ERRORS ]

/* Data load with transformation */
COPY INTO [<namespace>.]<table_name> [ ( <col_name> [ , <col_name> ... ] ) ]
     FROM ( SELECT [<alias>.]$<file_col_num>[.<element>] [ , [<alias>.]$<file_col_num>[.<element>] ... ]
            FROM { internalStage | externalStage } )
[ FILES = ( '<file_name>' [ , '<file_name>' ] [ , ... ] ) ]
[ PATTERN = '<regex_pattern>' ]
[ FILE_FORMAT = ( { FORMAT_NAME = '[<namespace>.]<file_format_name>' |

[ copyOptions ]

Create an Azure stage
A stage specifies where data files are stored (that is, ΓÇ£stagedΓÇ¥) so that the data in the files can be loaded into a table.
Data can be loaded directly from files in a specified Azure container or in an Azure ΓÇ£folderΓÇ¥ path (i.e. key value prefix). If the path ends with /, all of the objects in the corresponding Azure folder are loaded.
External stages
In addition to loading directly from files in Azure containers, Snowflake supports creating named external stages, which encapsulate all of the required information for staging files, including:

The Azure container where the files are staged.
The named storage integration object or Azure credentials for the container (if it is protected).
An encryption key (if the files in the container have been encrypted).

Named external stages are optional, but recommended when you plan to load data regularly from the same location. For instructions for creating an external stage, see Create an external stage below.
Note
To improve query performance for an Azure external stage, configure your network routing to use
Microsoft network routing.
For instructions, see the Azure documentation.
Create an external stage
You can create a named external stage using SQL or the web interface.

NoteTo create a stage, you must use a role that is granted or inherits the necessary privileges.
For more information, see Access control requirements for CREATE STAGE.
Create an external stage using SQL
Use the CREATE STAGE command to create an external stage.
The following example creates an external stage named my_azure_stage. The CREATE statement includes the azure_int storage
integration that was created in Configure an Azure container for loading data to access the Azure container container1 in the myaccount
account.
The data files are stored in the load/files/ path. The stage references a named file format object named my_csv_format, which
describes the data in the files stored in the path:
Copy codeCREATE STAGE my_azure_stage
  STORAGE_INTEGRATION = azure_int
  URL = 'azure://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer/load/files/'
  FILE_FORMAT = my_csv_format;

NoteUse the blob.core.windows.net endpoint for all supported types of Azure blob storage accounts, including Data Lake Storage Gen2.
NoteBy specifying a named file format object (or individual file format options) for the stage, it is not necessary to later specify the same file format options in the COPY command used to load data from
the stage. For more information about file format objects and options, see CREATE FILE FORMAT.
Create an external stage using Python
Use the StageCollection.create
method of the Snowflake Python APIs to create an external stage.
Similar to the preceding SQL example, the following Python example creates an external stage named my_azure_stage:
Copy codefrom snowflake.core.stage import Stage

my_stage = Stage(
  name="my_azure_stage",
  storage_integration="azure_int",
  url="azure://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer/load/files/"
)
root.databases["<database>"].schemas["<schema>"].stages.create(my_stage)

NoteThe Python API currently does not support the FILE_FORMAT parameter of the CREATE STAGE SQL command.
Create an external stage using Snowsight
To use Snowsight to create a named external stage, do the following:


sign in to Snowsight.


at the top of the navigation menu, select  (Create) ┬╗ Stage ┬╗ External Stage.


Select your external cloud storage provider: Amazon S3, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud Platform.


In the Create Stage dialog, enter a Stage Name.


Select the database and schema where you want to create the stage.


Enter the URL of your external cloud storage location.


If your external storage isnΓÇÖt public, enable Authentication and enter your details. For more information,
see CREATE STAGE.


Optionally deselect Directory table. Directory tables let you see files on the stage,
but require a warehouse and thus incur a cost. You can choose to deselect this option for now and enable a directory table later.
If you enable Directory table, optionally select Enable auto-refresh, and then select your event notification or
notification integration to automatically refresh the directory table when files are added or removed.
For more information, see Data Load Dirtables Auto.


If your files are encrypted, enable Encryption, and then enter your details.


(Optional) To view a generated SQL statement, expand the SQL Preview.
To specify additional options for your stage, such as AUTO_REFRESH, you can open this SQL preview in a worksheet.


Select Create.

Configure an Azure container for loading data
Configure secure access to data files stored in a Microsoft Azure container.
Snowflake supports the following options:
Option 1:Configure a storage integration object to delegate authentication responsibility for external cloud storage to an Azure service principal. A service principal is an identity created for use with services such as Snowflake to access Azure resources.This option makes it easier to manage access for multiple users
to different resources in Azure storage. A storage integration stores your secrets
so that you donΓÇÖt need to supply a SAS token every time you create an external stage.Note
Accessing Azure blob storage in government regions using a storage integration is limited to Snowflake
accounts hosted on Azure in the same government region. Accessing your blob storage from an account hosted outside of the government
region using direct credentials is supported.
Confirm that Snowflake supports the Azure region that your storage is hosted in. For more information, see
Supported cloud regions.
Option 2:Generate a shared access signature (SAS) token to grant Snowflake limited access to objects in your storage account. You can then access an external (Azure) stage that references the container using the SAS token.
Note
For the OneLake URL format, see CREATE STAGE.
Completing the instructions in this topic requires Azure administrative access. If youΓÇÖre not an Azure administrator,
ask your Azure administrator to perform these tasks.


To improve query performance for an Azure external stage, configure your network routing to use
Microsoft network routing.
For instructions, see the Azure documentation.



Option 1: Configure a Snowflake storage integration
This section describes how to use storage integrations to allow Snowflake to read data from and write data to an Azure container referenced in an external (Azure) stage. Integrations are named, first-class Snowflake objects that avoid the need for passing explicit cloud provider credentials such as secret keys or access tokens. Integration objects store an Azure identity and access management (IAM) user ID called the app registration. An administrator in your organization grants this app the necessary permissions in the Azure account.
An integration must also specify containers (and optional paths) that limit the locations users can specify when creating external stages that use the integration.
NoteCompleting the instructions in this section requires permissions in Azure to manage storage accounts. If you are not an Azure administrator, ask your Azure administrator to perform these tasks.
In this Section:
Step 1: Create a cloud storage integration in Snowflake
Create a storage integration using the CREATE STORAGE INTEGRATION command. A storage integration is a Snowflake object that stores a generated service principal for your Azure cloud storage, along with an optional set of allowed or blocked storage locations (that is, containers). Cloud provider administrators in your organization grant permissions on the storage locations to the generated service principal. This option allows users to avoid supplying credentials when creating stages or loading data.
A single storage integration can support multiple external (that is, Azure) stages. The URL in the stage definition must align with the Azure containers (and optional paths) specified for the STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS parameter.
NoteOnly account administrators (users with the ACCOUNTADMIN role) or a role with the global CREATE INTEGRATION privilege can execute this SQL command.
Copy codeCREATE STORAGE INTEGRATION <integration_name>
  TYPE = EXTERNAL_STAGE
  STORAGE_PROVIDER = 'AZURE'
  ENABLED = TRUE

Here is the deep dive, grounded in verified Snowflake capabilities and real marketplace listings. No guesswork ΓÇö every data source, ingestion path, storage model, transformation, and signal detection approach is traceable to a documented Snowflake feature or a publicly available data source.

---

## The design principle: complement, do not compete

The copilot **does not replace** the Core Banking System, the Loan Management System, or the Transaction Monitoring System. Those systems continue to do what they do well ΓÇö process transactions, manage loans, fire rule-based alerts. The copilot sits **downstream**, consuming their outputs through well-defined extraction points, and does what they cannot: join across silos, maintain an evidence chain, structure policy text, and produce audit-ready artifacts.

The positioning is: **the CBS is the system of record; the TMS is the detection engine; the copilot is the investigation, reasoning, and reporting layer that bridges them.**

---

## Data source architecture ΓÇö the complete map

There are four categories of data source, each with a different ingestion method, refresh cadence, storage model, and transformation pipeline. I will be explicit about every choice.

---

### Category 1: Transactional data from the CBS

**What it is:** The transaction feed ΓÇö every debit, credit, transfer, payment, cash withdrawal, and card transaction posted by the Core Banking System. This is the highest-volume, highest-velocity data source.

**What we extract (not the raw CBS schema ΓÇö a conformed extraction):**

| Field | Why |
|---|---|
| `txn_id` | Unique identifier, our primary key |
| `account_id` | Debit account |
| `counterparty_account_id` | Credit account (or external identifier) |
| `txn_timestamp` | Exact posting time |
| `amount` | In original currency |
| `currency` | ISO 4217 |
| `txn_type` | CREDIT, DEBIT, TRANSFER, CASH_DEPOSIT, CASH_WITHDRAWAL, CARD_PAYMENT, etc. |
| `channel` | BRANCH, ATM, MOBILE, INTERNET, POS, SWIFT, NEFT, RTGS, UPI, IMPS |
| `merchant_category_code` | For card transactions |
| `geo_lat, geo_lon` | For geolocated channels (ATM, POS) |
| `device_fingerprint` | For digital channels |
| `ip_address` | For internet/mobile channels |
| `reference_text` | Free text narration |

**Ingestion mechanism:** **Snowpipe Streaming (High-Performance Architecture).**

This is not a hypothetical choice. Snowpipe Streaming is GA on AWS with documented capabilities:
- Up to 20 GB/s throughput per table
- As low as 5 seconds ingest-to-queryable latency
- Elastic Channels for at-least-once delivery (suitable for transaction monitoring where we can deduplicate)
- Named Channels with offset tokens for exactly-once delivery (suitable if the CBS publishes via Kafka)
- In-flight transformations via COPY command syntax within the PIPE object ΓÇö we can reorder columns, cast types, and apply expressions before data is committed
- Schema evolution ΓÇö new columns detected in the stream are added without manual DDL

**Why Snowpipe Streaming and not batch COPY INTO:** Fraud detection requires seconds-to-minutes latency. A nightly batch extract would mean a transaction that fires at 9:01 AM is not visible until the next morning. The TMS sees it in real time; our copilot must see it within seconds to be useful for real-time alert enrichment.

**Storage:** Landing table `RAW_TRANSACTIONS`, append-only. This is the immutable audit spine. No updates, no deletes. Time Travel provides point-in-time access for evidence reproduction.

**Transformation ΓÇö the fast lane:**

Each dynamic table uses `REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL` (confirmed supported for joins, aggregations, and window functions in the Snowflake documentation). The pipeline is entirely declarative ΓÇö no tasks, no stored procedures, no imperative code to maintain.

**Critical design choice: why dynamic tables and not streams + tasks here.**

The Snowflake decision guide explicitly states: "Dynamic tables are the recommended approach for new multi-table SQL pipelines, especially pipelines with joins, aggregations, or window functions." Our velocity features are exactly this ΓÇö window functions over the transaction spine joined to dimension tables. Dynamic tables handle dependency ordering, incremental refresh, and skip-if-no-change automatically.

We use streams + tasks only where dynamic tables cannot go ΓÇö specifically, for side effects: sending notifications, calling external APIs, and writing to the `Case` table with procedural logic (IF/ELSE on signal severity). This is the documented hybrid pattern: `dynamic table ΓåÆ stream ΓåÆ triggered task ΓåÆ target`.

### Category 4: Regulatory and policy text ΓÇö the unstructured layer

This is the most architecturally novel data source. No other system treats regulatory text as structured, effective-dated, queryable data.

**4a. RBI Circulars and Master Directions**

RBI publishes circulars and Master Directions as PDFs on their website. These contain the actual regulatory rules: thresholds, timelines, reporting requirements, classification criteria.

**What we extract from each circular:**

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| `clause_id` | Auto-generated, stable across versions |
| `source_document` | "Master Direction ΓÇô Monitoring of Frauds in NBFCs (Ref. No. RBI/2024-25/XX)" |
| `source_page` | 12 |
| `section_heading` | "Classification of Frauds" |
| `clause_text` | "Fraud cases involving amounts of Γé╣1 lakh and above but less than Γé╣25 lakh shall be classified as Category B" |
| `effective_from` | 2024-04-01 |
| `effective_to` | NULL (current) |
| `applicability` | NBFC-ML, NBFC-UL |
| `metric` | fraud_amount |
| `operator` | BETWEEN |
| `threshold_lower` | 100000 |
| `threshold_upper` | 2500000 |
| `action_required` | "Report to RBI within 21 days" |
| `supersedes_clause_id` | Previous version's clause_id |

**Ingestion pipeline:**

```
INTERNAL STAGE @POLICY_DOCS
    Γöé (PDF uploaded manually or via scheduled download)
    Γû╝
TASK: PARSE_NEW_CIRCULARS (triggered when new files land on stage)
    Γöé
    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT(TO_FILE('@POLICY_DOCS', filename), 
    Γöé       {'mode': 'LAYOUT', 'page_split': true})
    Γöé   ΓåÆ Markdown text with tables and headers preserved
    Γöé
    Γö£ΓöÇΓöÇ AI_EXTRACT(parsed_text, 
    Γöé       'Extract all regulatory rules, thresholds, timelines,
    Γöé        classification criteria, and reporting requirements.
    Γöé        For each, return: section, clause_text, entity_type
    Γöé        it applies to, metric, operator, threshold_value,
    Γöé        effective_date, action_required')
    Γöé   ΓåÆ Structured JSON array of clause objects
    Γöé
    Γû╝
RAW_POLICY_CLAUSES (staging table)
    Γöé
    Γû╝
TASK: DIFF_AND_PROPOSE
    Γöé - Compare extracted clauses to current POLICY_CLAUSE table
    Γöé - Identify: NEW clauses, CHANGED thresholds, SUPERSEDED clauses
    Γöé - Write to POLICY_CHANGE_PROPOSALS (review queue)
    Γöé - DO NOT activate ΓÇö human approval required
    Γöé
    Γû╝
[HUMAN REVIEW via Streamlit or Slack MCP]
    Γöé - Compliance officer reviews proposed changes
    Γöé - Approves or rejects each
    Γöé - On approval: INSERT into POLICY_CLAUSE with effective_from
    Γöé   from the circular, set effective_to on superseded clause
    Γöé
    Γû╝
POLICY_CLAUSE (the governed, versioned rule table)
```

**Why AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT + AI_EXTRACT and not just RAG:** RAG returns paragraphs. A paragraph is not queryable ΓÇö you cannot ask "which controls have a threshold that just changed?" over a paragraph. The extraction produces **structured fields** with operators and thresholds that can be joined to detection rules. This is the difference between "policy as context" (weak) and "policy as data" (strong), as described in the solution plan ┬º3.3.

**4b. FIU-IND reporting templates**

FIU-IND publishes reporting formats for CTR, STR, CCR, NTR, CBWTR. These are structured templates with defined fields.

These templates are what the artifact generation agent uses to structure its output. When the agent drafts an STR, it writes to the `narrative_structure` defined here ΓÇö ensuring the output matches what FIU-IND expects.

## Signal detection ΓÇö how it works without competing with the TMS

The copilot does not replicate TMS rules. It does two things the TMS cannot:

**1. Cross-domain signals (the TMS cannot see across its own boundaries):**

| Signal | What it detects | Data sources joined | Why the TMS cannot do this |
|---|---|---|---|
| `INCOME_ACTIVITY_MISMATCH` | Inflows in 30d > N├ù declared annual income | Transactions + KYC | TMS does not have declared income |
| `SHARED_ATTRIBUTE_CLUSTER` | 3+ accounts sharing phone/device/IP with fund flows between them | PartyRelationship graph | TMS has no graph model |
| `MULE_RING_CANDIDATE` | Depth-3 fund-flow cycle through shared-attribute nodes | Recursive CTE over PartyRelationship | TMS cannot do graph traversal |
| `FRAUD_BORROWER_OVERLAP` | Borrower with open exposure AND fraud/AML signals | Exposures + Cases | TMS has no credit data |
| `SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW` | Customer or counterparty matches newly added sanctions entry | DIM_PARTY + SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED | Some TMS do this; ours adds context (all accounts, all transactions, exposure) |
| `PEP_TRANSACTION_ANOMALY` | PEP customer with transaction pattern inconsistent with declared source of funds | Transactions + KYC + PEP list | TMS may flag PEP transactions but cannot compare to declared income/SOF |
| `STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT` | Sub-threshold transactions split across multiple accounts owned by the same party | Transactions joined via DIM_PARTY | TMS is typically account-level, not party-level |

**2. Enrichment of TMS alerts (the copilot makes the TMS's output more useful):**

If the TMS fires an alert, the copilot can ingest that alert (via a daily/intra-day batch from the TMS alert export) and enrich it with everything the TMS does not include:
- Full customer profile and KYC history
- Network analysis (who else is connected to this account?)
- Credit exposure (is this person also a borrower? What stage?)
- Prior cases and dispositions on this customer
- Applicable policy clauses and thresholds

This enrichment is what replaces steps 4-8 of Process A (the manual data gathering described in the target users analysis). The TMS fires the alert; the copilot provides the investigation context.

**The graph query ΓÇö mule ring detection (recursive CTE):**

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE ring_search AS (
    -- Seed: the account under investigation
    SELECT 
        account_id AS start_account,
        counterparty_account_id AS current_account,
        1 AS depth,
        ARRAY_CONSTRUCT(account_id, counterparty_account_id) AS path
    FROM DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP
    WHERE account_id = :seed_account
      AND relationship_type = 'FUND_FLOW'
      AND total_amount > :min_flow_threshold
    
    UNION ALL
    
    -- Traverse: follow fund flows up to depth 3
    SELECT 
        rs.start_account,
        pr.counterparty_account_id,
        rs.depth + 1,
        ARRAY_APPEND(rs.path, pr.counterparty_account_id)
    FROM ring_search rs
    JOIN DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP pr
        ON rs.current_account = pr.account_id
        AND pr.relationship_type = 'FUND_FLOW'
        AND pr.total_amount > :min_flow_threshold
    WHERE rs.depth < 3
      AND NOT ARRAY_CONTAINS(pr.counterparty_account_id::VARIANT, rs.path)
)
SELECT * FROM ring_search
WHERE current_account = start_account  -- cycle detected
   OR EXISTS (
       -- shared non-financial attribute between path members
       SELECT 1 FROM DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP shared
       WHERE shared.relationship_type IN ('SHARED_PHONE','SHARED_DEVICE','SHARED_ADDRESS')
         AND ARRAY_CONTAINS(shared.account_id::VARIANT, path)
         AND ARRAY_CONTAINS(shared.counterparty_account_id::VARIANT, path)
   );
```

This is bounded (depth 3), guards against cycles (path check), and combines fund-flow traversal with shared-attribute detection. The TMS cannot express this ΓÇö it has no recursive traversal, no graph edges, and no shared-attribute data.

## Notification ΓÇö from signal to action

Signals alone are insufficient. The copilot must route signals to the right person at the right time.

**Design: stream on DT_SIGNALS_FAST ΓåÆ triggered task ΓåÆ notification routing:**

```
STREAM: SIGNALS_STREAM ON DYNAMIC TABLE DT_SIGNALS_FAST

TASK: ROUTE_SIGNALS
    WAREHOUSE = signal_wh
    WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('SIGNALS_STREAM')
AS
    -- For each new signal:
    -- 1. Check if an open case already exists for this party
    --    If yes: attach signal to existing case
    --    If no and severity >= threshold: create new case
    -- 2. Route notification based on signal type:
    --    FRAUD signals ΓåÆ Slack #fraud-ops channel (MCP)
    --    AML signals ΓåÆ compliance team queue
    --    CROSS_DOMAIN signals ΓåÆ both + CRO dashboard
    -- 3. Write to CASE and SIGNAL tables
    -- 4. For SANCTIONS_MATCH: immediate high-priority alert
```

This is the documented hybrid pattern: dynamic table (declarative computation) ΓåÆ stream (capture changes) ΓåÆ task (procedural routing with side effects). The task fires only when the stream has unconsumed changes, so no polling and no wasted compute.

## What this design does NOT do (boundaries stated explicitly)

1. **Does not replace the CBS.** Does not process or post transactions. Consumes CBS output.
2. **Does not replace the TMS.** Does not make real-time block/allow decisions on transactions. The TMS continues to do that. The copilot enriches TMS alerts and adds cross-domain signals the TMS cannot compute.
3. **Does not replace the LMS.** Does not manage loans, compute interest, or process repayments. Consumes LMS exposure snapshots.
4. **Does not replace KYC operations.** Does not onboard customers or conduct due diligence. Consumes the output of the KYC platform.
5. **Does not auto-activate regulatory changes.** New circulars are parsed and proposed; a human approves activation.
6. **Does not file STRs autonomously.** Generates drafts; a human attests and files.
7. **Does not ingest real customer data.** The entire dataset is synthetic. Production data sources are documented as integration points with exact field mappings, not as working connections.

Every ingestion path, transformation rule, and detection signal is traceable to a documented Snowflake feature, a publicly available data source, or a confirmed Marketplace listing.

# Data Sources Deep Dive ΓÇö Risk & Compliance Copilot

**Session date:** 2026-09-20
**Purpose:** Complete data source architecture ΓÇö ingestion, storage, transformation, signal detection, and notification. Grounded in verified Snowflake capabilities and confirmed Marketplace listings. No guesswork.

---

## Design Principle: Complement, Do Not Compete

The copilot does not replace the Core Banking System, the Loan Management System, or the Transaction Monitoring System. Those systems continue to do what they do well ΓÇö process transactions, manage loans, fire rule-based alerts. The copilot sits downstream, consuming their outputs through well-defined extraction points, and does what they cannot: join across silos, maintain an evidence chain, structure policy text, and produce audit-ready artifacts.

**The CBS is the system of record. The TMS is the detection engine. The copilot is the investigation, reasoning, and reporting layer that bridges them.**

---

## Data Source Architecture ΓÇö Four Categories

### Category 1: Transactional Data from CBS

**Extraction schema (conformed, not raw CBS):**

| Field | Why |
|---|---|
| txn_id | Unique identifier, primary key |
| account_id | Debit account |
| counterparty_account_id | Credit account or external identifier |
| txn_timestamp | Exact posting time |
| amount | In original currency |
| currency | ISO 4217 |
| txn_type | CREDIT, DEBIT, TRANSFER, CASH_DEPOSIT, CASH_WITHDRAWAL, CARD_PAYMENT |
| channel | BRANCH, ATM, MOBILE, INTERNET, POS, SWIFT, NEFT, RTGS, UPI, IMPS |
| merchant_category_code | For card transactions |
| geo_lat, geo_lon | For geolocated channels |
| device_fingerprint | For digital channels |
| ip_address | For internet/mobile channels |
| reference_text | Free text narration |

**Ingestion: Snowpipe Streaming (High-Performance Architecture)**
- Up to 20 GB/s throughput per table
- As low as 5 seconds ingest-to-queryable latency
- Elastic Channels for at-least-once delivery (deduplicate downstream)
- Named Channels with offset tokens for exactly-once (Kafka sources)
- In-flight transformations via COPY command syntax in PIPE object
- Schema evolution ΓÇö new columns added without manual DDL

**Storage:** Landing table RAW_TRANSACTIONS, append-only. Immutable audit spine. Time Travel for point-in-time evidence reproduction.

**Transformation ΓÇö Fast Lane (Dynamic Tables):**

```
RAW_TRANSACTIONS (landing, Snowpipe Streaming)
    |
    v
DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED (TARGET_LAG = '1 minute')
    - Joins to DIM_ACCOUNT, DIM_PARTY for customer context
    - Computes: is_round_amount, is_just_below_threshold flags
    - Tags channel type and geo region
    |
    v
DT_TXN_VELOCITY_FEATURES (TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes')
    - Per-account rolling features:
      - 1h/24h/7d/30d transaction count and sum
      - Distinct counterparty count per window
      - Channel entropy
      - Time-of-day distribution deviation
      - Max single txn as % of 30d average
    |
    v
DT_SIGNALS_FAST (TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes')
    - Detection rules over velocity features
    - Output: signal_id, party_id, account_id, rule_id,
              fired_at, severity, evidence_txn_ids, as_of_ts
```

All dynamic tables use REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL (supported for joins, aggregations, window functions per Snowflake docs).

---

### Category 2: Entity and Relationship Data (CBS + KYC Platform)

**2a. Party (Customer Master)**

| Field | Source | Why |

| party_id | CBS customer ID | Entity resolution anchor |
| party_type | CBS | INDIVIDUAL, CORPORATE, TRUST, HUF |
| full_name | CBS | Display and search |
| date_of_birth / incorporation_date | CBS | Age-based risk, sanctions matching |
| nationality / jurisdiction | KYC | FATF jurisdiction risk |
| occupation / business_type | KYC | Expected transaction profile |
| declared_annual_income | KYC | Income-vs-activity mismatch detection |
| risk_rating | KYC | HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW |
| pep_flag | KYC / PEP screening | AML risk scoring |
| kyc_status | KYC | VERIFIED / PENDING / EXPIRED |
| source_of_funds | KYC | Comparison against actual flows |
| beneficial_owner_party_ids | KYC | Ownership chain for UBO analysis |

**2b. PartyRelationship ΓÇö Graph Spine**

Constructed from multiple sources during ingestion:

| Relationship type | Source |
|---|---|
| OWNS_ACCOUNT | CBS |
| BENEFICIAL_OWNER_OF | KYC (UBO chain) |
| DIRECTOR_OF | KYC / MCA filings |
| SHARED_PHONE | KYC onboarding data |
| SHARED_ADDRESS | KYC onboarding data |
| SHARED_DEVICE | Digital banking platform |
| SHARED_IP | Digital banking platform |
| FUND_FLOW | Derived from transactions (aggregated) |
| GUARANTOR_OF | LMS |
| CO_BORROWER | LMS |

**2c. Account Master**

| Field | Source |

| account_id | CBS |
| party_id | CBS (FK to DIM_PARTY) |
| account_type | SAVINGS, CURRENT, LOAN, CREDIT_CARD, FIXED_DEPOSIT |
| opened_date | CBS |
| status | ACTIVE, DORMANT, FROZEN, CLOSED |
| current_balance | CBS (daily snapshot) |
| credit_limit | CBS (credit accounts) |

**Ingestion:** Daily batch COPY INTO from CBS/KYC exports (CSV/JSON to stage).

**Transformation:**

```
RAW_PARTY_CBS + RAW_PARTY_KYC
    |
    v
DT_DIM_PARTY (TARGET_LAG = '1 day')
    - Entity resolution: match CBS customer to KYC record
    - Resolve duplicates (same PAN, same phone + DOB)
    - Output: one conformed row per party with match_confidence

DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP (TARGET_LAG = '1 day')

    - FUND_FLOW edges derived from DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED
```

Balance snapshots stored as SCD Type 2 (daily insert with as_of_date) to support point-in-time balance lookups for evidence reproduction.

4. DT_SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED (dynamic table, TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM)

**Decision:** Ingest real UN and OFAC lists directly (free, public, strong credibility). Supplement with TRUVITY PEP dataset from Marketplace (demonstrates Marketplace integration).

#### 3b. FATF High-Risk and Monitored Jurisdictions

#### 3c. IP Intelligence

#### 3e. Adverse Media

TRUVITY Adverse Media (GZSYZMQ0QY) confirmed on Marketplace. For production, RavenPack News Analytics (GZTSZ9DN1IO) provides structured sentiment from 40,000+ news sources (commercial).

---

### Category 4: Regulatory and Policy Text

**4a. RBI Circulars and Master Directions**

Extraction schema for POLICY_CLAUSE:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| clause_id | Auto-generated, stable across versions |
| source_document | "Master Direction - Monitoring of Frauds in NBFCs (Ref. No. RBI/2024-25/XX)" |
| source_page | 12 |
| section_heading | "Classification of Frauds" |
| clause_text | Full clause text |
| effective_from | 2024-04-01 |
| effective_to | NULL (current) |
| applicability | NBFC-ML, NBFC-UL |

| threshold_lower | 100000 |
| threshold_upper | 2500000 |
| action_required | "Report to RBI within 21 days" |
| supersedes_clause_id | Previous version's clause_id |

**Ingestion pipeline:**

```
INTERNAL STAGE @POLICY_DOCS
    | (PDF uploaded or scheduled download)
    v
TASK: PARSE_NEW_CIRCULARS
    |
    |- AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT(TO_FILE('@POLICY_DOCS', filename),
    |      {'mode': 'LAYOUT', 'page_split': true})
    |  -> Markdown with tables and headers preserved
    |
    |- AI_EXTRACT(parsed_text,
    |      'Extract all regulatory rules, thresholds, timelines...')
    |  -> Structured JSON array of clause objects
    v
RAW_POLICY_CLAUSES (staging)
    v
TASK: DIFF_AND_PROPOSE
    - Compare to current POLICY_CLAUSE
    - Identify NEW, CHANGED, SUPERSEDED
    - Write to POLICY_CHANGE_PROPOSALS (review queue)
    - DO NOT activate
    v
[HUMAN REVIEW]
    - Approves or rejects each proposal
    - On approval: INSERT into POLICY_CLAUSE with effective_from
    v
POLICY_CLAUSE (governed, versioned rule table)
```

**4b. FIU-IND Reporting Templates**

```
REF_FILING_TEMPLATES
    - template_id

    - version
    - effective_from

```

### Category 5: Credit Exposure Data from LMS

|---|---|
| loan_account_id | Primary key |
| party_id | FK to DIM_PARTY (cross-silo join key) |
| product_type | TERM_LOAN, WORKING_CAPITAL, OVERDRAFT, GOLD_LOAN |
| sanctioned_amount | Original loan amount |
| outstanding_principal | Current balance |
| dpd | Days past due |

| restructured_flag | Whether restructured |
| npa_date | Date classified as NPA |

**Ingestion:** Daily batch COPY INTO from LMS export.

**Transformation ΓÇö Slow Lane:**

```
RAW_EXPOSURES (daily batch)
    |
    v
DT_EXPOSURES_STAGED (TARGET_LAG = '1 day')
    - Compute DPD, classify SMA-0/1/2, NPA
    - Sub-classify NPA: SUBSTANDARD/DOUBTFUL/LOSS
    - Thresholds from POLICY_CLAUSE table
    - Join to DT_DIM_PARTY
    - Flag: has_open_fraud_case, has_aml_alert (from CASE table)
    |
    v
DT_EXPOSURE_PORTFOLIO (TARGET_LAG = '1 day')
    - Total outstanding by stage
    - Migration matrix
    - Sector concentration
    - Large exposure flags
    |
    v
DT_PROVISIONING (TARGET_LAG = '1 day')
    - ECL: Stage 1 (12m PD x LGD x EAD),
           Stage 2 (Lifetime PD x LGD x EAD),
           Stage 3 (Lifetime PD x LGD x (EAD - collateral))
    - PD/LGD from POLICY_CLAUSE
```

**The cross-silo bridge:** DT_EXPOSURES_STAGED joins to CASE table to check whether borrower has open fraud/AML cases. This is the join no existing system makes.

---

### Category 6: Balance Sheet Data for Liquidity (If Scope Permits)

| Field | Why |

| gl_code | General ledger account code |
| balance | As-of-date balance |
| maturity_date | For bucketing |
| lcr_classification | HQLA_L1/L2A/L2B, OUTFLOW_RETAIL/WHOLESALE, INFLOW |
| haircut_rate | From POLICY_CLAUSE |
| runoff_rate | From POLICY_CLAUSE |

**Transformation:**

```
DT_LCR_COMPUTATION (TARGET_LAG = '1 day')
    - HQLA = SUM(balance * (1 - haircut_rate))
    - Outflows = SUM(balance * runoff_rate)
    - Inflows = SUM(balance * inflow_rate), capped at 75% of outflows
    - LCR = HQLA / (Outflows - Inflows)
    - Haircuts/runoff rates joined from POLICY_CLAUSE (effective-dated)
```

## Signal Detection ΓÇö Cross-Domain (What the TMS Cannot Do)

| INCOME_ACTIVITY_MISMATCH | Inflows in 30d > Nx declared annual income | Transactions + KYC | TMS lacks declared income |
| SHARED_ATTRIBUTE_CLUSTER | 3+ accounts sharing phone/device/IP with fund flows | PartyRelationship graph | TMS has no graph model |
| MULE_RING_CANDIDATE | Depth-3 fund-flow cycle through shared-attribute nodes | Recursive CTE over PartyRelationship | TMS cannot do graph traversal |
| FRAUD_BORROWER_OVERLAP | Borrower with exposure AND fraud/AML signals | Exposures + Cases | TMS has no credit data |
| SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW | Customer matches newly added sanctions entry | DIM_PARTY + SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED | Copilot adds full context |
| PEP_TRANSACTION_ANOMALY | PEP with transactions inconsistent with declared SOF | Transactions + KYC + PEP list | TMS cannot compare to SOF |
| STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT | Sub-threshold txns split across accounts of same party | Transactions via DIM_PARTY | TMS is account-level, not party-level |

# Architecture Diagrams & Visual Design Session

**Session date:** 2026-09-21
**Purpose:** Convert the dense text-based data sources analysis into visual Mermaid diagrams for the entire Risk & Compliance Copilot architecture. Created after user feedback that the prior text-heavy document was too difficult to parse.

---

## Decision: Mermaid over FigJam

**Considered:** FigJam connector, Mermaid, draw.io, PlantUML
**Chosen:** Mermaid ΓÇö renders natively in GitHub, VS Code, Streamlit, and most markdown viewers. No external tool, no export step, no account required. Least effort, best quality.

---

## Diagrams Created (12 total)

All in `docs/architecture-diagrams.md`:

1. **Entity Relationship Model** ΓÇö 13 entities (Party, Account, Transaction, PartyRelationship, Exposure, Signal, Case, Evidence, Finding, PolicyClause, Artifact, Attestation, SanctionsEntry) with full field lists and relationship cardinalities.

2. **Data Ingestion Architecture** ΓÇö Color-coded by method:
   - Blue: Snowpipe Streaming (CBS transactions, 5s latency)
   - Purple: Batch COPY INTO (KYC, LMS, GL ΓÇö daily)
   - Green: HTTP GET via External Access Integration (sanctions lists ΓÇö daily)
   - Orange: Marketplace zero-copy share (TRUVITY PEP, IPinfo, MaxMind)
   - Red: AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT + AI_EXTRACT (RBI circulars ΓÇö on demand)

3. **Two-Speed Transformation Pipeline** ΓÇö Fast lane (DT_TRANSACTIONS_ENRICHED at 1 min, DT_TXN_VELOCITY_FEATURES at 5 min, DT_SIGNALS_FAST at 5 min) and slow lane (DT_EXPOSURES_STAGED, DT_EXPOSURE_PORTFOLIO, DT_PROVISIONING all at 1 day), with shared dimensions (DT_DIM_PARTY, DT_PARTY_RELATIONSHIP, DT_SANCTIONS_CONSOLIDATED, POLICY_CLAUSE) feeding both.

4. **Signal-to-Artifact Pipeline** ΓÇö The 7-stage evidence chain: Detect -> Group -> Gather -> Reason -> Draft -> Review -> Attest. Shows adversarial reviewer feedback loop (reject -> re-draft).

5. **Cross-Domain Signal Detection** ΓÇö 7 signals the TMS cannot compute (INCOME_ACTIVITY_MISMATCH, SHARED_ATTRIBUTE_CLUSTER, MULE_RING_CANDIDATE, STRUCTURING_CROSS_ACCOUNT, PEP_TRANSACTION_ANOMALY, FRAUD_BORROWER_OVERLAP, SANCTIONS_MATCH_NEW), with data source inputs for each.

6. **Notification and Case Routing** ΓÇö Stream on DT_SIGNALS_FAST -> ROUTE_SIGNALS task -> decision logic (existing case? severity threshold?) -> channel routing (Slack #fraud-ops, compliance queue, CRO dashboard, immediate alert for sanctions).

7. **Policy Ingestion Pipeline** ΓÇö PDF -> AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT -> AI_EXTRACT -> staging -> diff -> review queue -> human approval -> POLICY_CLAUSE. Human-gated. Shows rejected path.

8. **Demo Spine** ΓÇö One entity (Rajesh Kumar, P-10042) across four lenses:
   - Fraud: velocity signals, shared device cluster, mule ring candidate
   - AML: case opened, graph query traces ring, STR drafted, MLRO attests
   - Credit: Rs 15L exposure at 42 DPD, staging moves to Stage 2, provisioning changes
   - Capital: exposure flows to CRAR, RWA increases, capital closer to floor

9. **External Data Sources** ΓÇö Public (UN, OFAC, EU, UK, MHA, FATF) vs Marketplace (TRUVITY, IPinfo, MaxMind, FactSet, OpenCorporates), ingestion method per source.

10. **Complete Storage Model** ΓÇö All tables in 4 categories: Immutable Landing (append-only), Dynamic Tables (Snowflake-managed), Governed State (human-gated), Evidence Chain (append-only audit trail).

11. **Target Users** ΓÇö Fraud Analyst, AML Compliance Officer, MLRO, Credit Risk Analyst, Treasury/ALM Officer mapped to copilot capabilities they use.

12. **System Boundary** ΓÇö Existing systems kept (CBS, TMS, LMS, KYC) vs copilot's new capabilities (cross-silo bridge, evidence chain, policy-as-data, audit-ready outputs). Shows data flow direction: existing systems feed the copilot.

---

## Key Design Decisions Reflected

- Two-speed architecture is visually explicit (diagram 3): fraud signals at 5-minute lag, balance sheet metrics at 1-day lag, shared dimensions serving both
- Evidence-as-pointers (not copies) is called out in diagram 4 and the ER model
- Human-gated policy activation is a separate diagram (7) emphasizing the review queue and reject path
- The demo spine (diagram 8) shows how one entity creates the narrative thread across all four pillars
- System boundary diagram (12) makes explicit that the copilot complements, not competes with, existing banking systems

---
